commits.commit_title: fix(codex): stop an unparseable Bash command from blocking the tool call (#4001)
commits.commit_message:
fix(codex): stop an unparseable Bash command from blocking the tool call (#4001)

`extractFromBash` calls shell-quote's `parse()` on every Bash PreToolUse
command to enrich the payload with `filePaths` for read commands. `parse()`
throws on substitutions it cannot resolve, the throw was not caught here, and
it reached the generic hook handler — which logs `Hook error:` and returns
BLOCKING_ERROR. A best-effort convenience field was turning an ordinary shell
command into a blocked tool call.

Reproduced against the version actually installed here, not just the 1.8.4 in
the report:

    shell-quote 1.10.0
    parse("cat ${}")               -> throws  Bad substitution: ${}
    parse("echo hi && cat ${}")    -> throws  Bad substitution: ${}

The trigger is an *empty* substitution. `${FOO}`, `${#FOO}`, `${FOO:?err}` and
`${arr[@]}` all parse fine on 1.10.0, which is why the form matters: the guard
is needed on current dependencies, not only on the older one.

It also matters that `plugin/scripts/worker-service.cjs` — the file that ships —
carries a bundled copy containing the same `Bad substitution` throw, so the
behaviour does not depend on what a fresh `npm install` resolves.

The parse is now guarded and yields no paths on failure. Failing to enrich is
invisible; blocking the user's command is not.

Three tests, two of which fail without the guard (7 pass / 2 fail):

  - an unparseable substitution yields [] instead of throwing
  - the same when it rides alongside a genuinely readable file, so the failure
    is attributable to tokenisation rather than to a bad path
  - a command that parses still extracts its paths — the guard must not
    swallow the feature it protects

`bun test tests/cli tests/hooks` — 116 passed.

The committed bundle is left alone: rebuilding it here diverges from the
committed artifact for unrelated reasons, so it should be regenerated by the
normal release build rather than by this PR.

Co-authored-by: Nguyen Thanh Dat <ntdat812@gmail.com>

commits.commit_title: fix(worker): make the LLM per-attempt deadline configurable and stop retrying it (#4000)
commits.commit_message:
fix(worker): make the LLM per-attempt deadline configurable and stop retrying it (#4000)

* fix(worker): make the LLM per-attempt deadline configurable and stop retrying it

The observer's per-attempt request deadline was hardcoded at 30s with no way
to reach it from configuration, and neither of the two withRetry call sites
passes an override. On a local model that truncates work that has already
been computed: a report on an Ollama backend measured a median of 21s and a
p99 of 29.8s against the 30s deadline, with every failure landing at exactly
30.000s. The workaround was editing the installed bundle after each update.

CLAUDE_MEM_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS now sets it, validated against the same 500..300000
bounds the other CLAUDE_MEM_*_TIMEOUT_MS settings use. Hosted providers keep
the 30s default and see no change.

A request aborted by that deadline is also no longer retried. The abort
surfaces with no HTTP status, so it classified as transient and ran two more
attempts against a backend that was already saturated, which is what turns a
latency problem into a congestion collapse. It now fails with a message
naming the deadline and the setting that raises it.

Refs #3794.

* fix(worker): reject suffixed CLAUDE_MEM_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS values

parseInt('90000ms') silently accepted a typo as 90000. Require a complete
integer so a bad setting warns and keeps the 30s default.

Co-authored-by: Alex Newman <thedotmack@users.noreply.github.com>

server: let CLAUDE_MEM_SERVER_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS set the generation output cap (#3997)

All three server generation providers already accept maxOutputTokens, but
nothing ever populated it, so every request went out with the constructor
default of 4096. On a model that answers at length the reply is truncated
mid-structure, the observation parser rejects it, and the job settles as a

Non-integer and non-positive values are ignored with a warning rather than
sent as NaN.

commits.commit_title: fix(context): fit the session block to the hook output limit by selection (#3995)
commits.commit_message:
fix(context): fit the session block to the hook output limit by selection (#3995)

* fix(context): fit the session block to the hook output limit by selection

Claude Code delivers a hook's stdout verbatim up to 10,000 characters, then
writes the whole block to disk and hands the model a ~2KB preview stub
instead -- while the hook still reports success. The context block was sized
by item counts, so on an active project it crossed that line and the model
silently received no context at all.

Counts cannot fix it: an observation title runs ~150-320 characters, a
session-summary line ~250-600, and the last-session summary block 1-5K on its
own, so any count safe on a quiet project wastes the budget and any count
that fills the budget there overflows on a busy one. The shipped default of
50 observations overflows on titles alone.

Measure instead. Render, and while the result is over budget drop the most
expensive thing still in it and render again: full narratives first (their
titles stay), then the last-session summary block, then sessions, then
observations. Whole items go, never half of one, so the block stays
well-formed and the header, footer and at least one observation survive.

--full is an explicit human request and is left unbounded.

Fixes #3802

* fix(context): count the health warning and report what was delivered

Addresses the three P1 findings on this PR. All three were real; the first two
are fixed here with tests, the third by rebuilding the two bundles that
actually carry the change.

**The observer-health warning is now inside the measured block.** It was
appended to the already-fitted text, so its characters were never counted: a
block fitted to 9,998 came back at 10,585 whenever the observer was unhealthy,
and over the limit Claude Code replaces the whole thing with the ~2KB preview
stub — losing the context *and* the outage warning, which is exactly when that
warning matters most.

`readObserverHealth` is now read once rather than per render. `fitContextToBudget`
calls its render repeatedly and that function touches state; re-reading it per
reduction would let the measured length move under the loop.

**Injection stats now describe the delivered block.** A run trimmed from seven
observations to three still reported `observation_count: 7` and 9,646 tokens
injected while the model received three observations and 4,134 tokens. That is
the one direction this telemetry must not be wrong in — it read as healthy
precisely when context was being dropped. `ContextInjectStats` already promised
this ("computed from the same observation set that was rendered"); the code now
matches its own contract. Summaries use `budget.config.sessionCount`, the same
slice `buildContextOutput` takes for `displaySummaries`.

Both live in a new exported `fitContextForDelivery`, split out of
`generateContextWithStats` so the fitting and the reporting can be tested
without a database — the module previously had no in-process test path at all,
which is why neither defect was caught.

**Bundles.** `plugin/scripts/worker-service.cjs` and
`plugin/scripts/context-generator.cjs` are rebuilt: marketplace hooks execute
the checked-in bundle, so the fix does not reach installs without them.

`mcp-server.cjs` and `server-service.cjs` are deliberately NOT included, and
that is measured rather than assumed. Rebuilding them from a clean tree
produces byte-identical output to rebuilding them with this patch applied, and
both differ from what is committed on `main` — so their diff is pre-existing
drift, not this change, and carrying it here would bury the review in noise.

Five cases in `tests/context/context-budget-3802.test.ts`, driven through
`fitContextForDelivery` rather than through `fitContextToBudget`, because both
defects were in what happens *around* the fitter.

The fixture is chosen so it can tell the two apart: 47 observations render to
9,900 characters, which fits, and 9,900 plus a 600-character warning does not.
An earlier version of this test used 50 observations and **passed under the
mutation** — the fitter's reductions are coarse, so the fitted block landed far
enough below the limit that a warning appended afterwards still fit. Measured,
then fixed.

- Moving the warning back outside the fitter fails
  `counts the observer-health warning against the budget`.
- Passing the original arrays to `buildInjectStats` fails two of the stats cases.

`bun test tests/context/` gives 83 pass / 4 fail; the four are
`context database ownership`, which fail identically on `main` (a child-process
stdout JSON parse, unrelated to this change). `bun run typecheck:root`,
`lint:hook-io` and `lint:spawn-env` are clean.

commits.commit_title: fix(provider): pause the session on a reactive quota error instead of ending it (#3999)
commits.commit_message:
fix(provider): pause the session on a reactive quota error instead of ending it (#3999)

* fix(provider): pause the session on a reactive quota error instead of ending it

session.abortReason was only ever set to a quota category by the two
proactive sites: the pre-request rate-limit guard, and the observer-text
heuristic. A 429 that comes back from the provider is classified correctly
and then rethrown with abortReason untouched, so the .finally() in
SessionRoutes reads null, handleGeneratorExit falls past its preserve list,
and finalizeSession drops whatever the session had buffered.

The reporter's log shows the tell directly: "Generator exited — finalizing
session {reason=null}", ten times in fifteen minutes, each one a separate
observation lost to a condition that cleared by itself.

handleSessionError now maps a classified failure onto the category that
keeps the work: quota_exhausted and rate_limit to quota, auth_invalid to
auth. Both categories are already honoured by handleGeneratorExit, so
nothing downstream needed to change. Everything else keeps finalizing —
a genuinely unrecoverable session should still be cleaned up.

The reason is recorded before the rethrow, since the .finally() that reads
it runs as the throw unwinds.

* fix(provider): abort the controller when pausing on a reactive quota error

Labelling the abort reason without aborting left the controller live while
the error unwound, so the session route booked an observer failure and an
error outcome on the way out and finalization booked the aborted outcome
after — a pause recorded twice, once as a failure, with observer-health
left marked failed.

The two observer-text paths already abort for the same conditions; this
matches them. Genuinely fatal errors still leave the controller alone.

---------

commits.commit_title: fix(observer): strip image payloads out of the observation prompt (#3996)
commits.commit_message:
fix(observer): strip image payloads out of the observation prompt (#3996)

* fix(observer): strip image payloads out of the observation prompt

A tool_result carrying a screenshot went into the observer prompt as raw
base64. Two things compound it. truncateObservationField keeps the head
and tail of an oversized field, so what survived a screenshot was
thousands of characters of base64 rather than the caption beside it; and
the prompt is appended to session.conversationHistory, which every later
observation in the session re-sends in full. A browser-automation session
taking a few hundred screenshots replays all of it, every time — which is
how single observations reached 400K-1M discovery_tokens against a 30K-50K
baseline.

Measured on one screenshot-shaped tool_result: the prompt goes from 15,460
characters with a 9,338-character contiguous base64 run to 1,277 characters
with none, and the text block beside the image is kept.

Stripping is generic, on the shape of the content block, rather than by
tool name. CLAUDE_MEM_SKIP_TOOLS needs every screenshot-producing tool
enumerated in advance, and it drops the whole observation rather than
keeping the part that has signal. Anthropic image blocks and OpenAI
image_url data: URLs are both elided, with the media type and byte count
reported so the observer can see something was there. A plain http image
URL is left alone: it is short and it carries signal.

* fix(observer): keep url-backed Anthropic image sources

The Anthropic branch replaced any object source, so an image block backed
by a plain https URL lost the URL and its metadata. The OpenAI branch
already made that distinction; this matches it. Only an inlined data:
payload is removed.

* fix(observer): treat DATA: URIs as inlined image payloads

URI schemes are case-insensitive. The lowercase-only data: check let an
uppercase DATA: screenshot through as thousands of characters of base64.

Co-authored-by: Alex Newman <thedotmack@users.noreply.github.com>

commits.commit_title: fix(windows): make the ghost gate's fixture handshake independent of stdout buffering (#3992)
commits.commit_message:
fix(windows): make the ghost gate's fixture handshake independent of stdout buffering (#3992)

* fix(windows): make the ghost gate's fixture handshake independent of stdout buffering

The revision landed as 155fefce (#3989) fixed the unbounded port probe, but the
gate it was meant to unblock still fails on CI. Every failing run has the same
shape: no stage output, exactly `2 expect() calls`, and the fixture's `ready`
line only visible once the fixture is killed at the 600s cap — while the
fixture's chroma chain is already alive 3s in. The handshake read a redirected
stdout, and a single small line written by a process that then idles can sit
unflushed in that buffer indefinitely.

The fixture now appends every event to an events file (a syscall per call —
nothing left to flush) and keeps the stdout copy for human debugging, plus
emits progress stages with elapsed times. The test reads readiness from the
file, prints `waiting for fixture ready: elapsed=… lastStage=…` every 15s so
the timeline survives even a bun-timeout kill, gives up at 240s (below bun's
cap) with the full events/stdout/stderr dump, and reaps an in-flight
ensureWorkerStarted() during teardown instead of leaving it running past
cleanup.

Locally the gate passes in 41.9s with the stage timeline visible: fixture ready
after 6.1s, ghost confirmed, ensureWorkerStarted 'ready' after 27.4s.

* test(windows): sweep stragglers an abandoned launcher leaves behind

The deadline race cannot cancel ensureWorkerStarted(), so teardown waits for it
— but that wait is time-boxed, and a launcher still mid-flight can spawn its
worker or reclaim the chain AFTER the kills. Fault-injection check (deadline
temporarily at 1s, which abandons the launcher mid-flight): teardown used to
leave a ghost listener on the port and a live isolated chroma chain behind
(ghost owner dead + 3 surviving sidecar processes). Teardown now repeats
"reap the pid-file worker, free the port via the production reclaim" in bounded
rounds until the port is quiet; the same injection now leaves zero listeners
and zero surviving isolated processes, and the green path still passes in 40s.

* test(windows): give the ghost gate's event channel a real contract

The events file this handshake reads was never written. `process.env.X = ...`
does not survive child_process in bun (children get the environment the
runner started with), so the fixture only ever emitted to stdout — and the
reader's stdout fallback hid that: every local run "passed" on the fallback
while CI, where redirected stdout is buffered, kept hanging. Probed:

  A bash-set env   -> child sees it
  B process.env.X  -> child does NOT see it
  C { ...process.env } passed explicitly -> child sees it

- pass the events file path as argv[2] instead (no env anywhere in the
  bun -> powershell -> Start-Process -> bun chain);
- stop reading stdout back: a broken channel must fail loudly, and stdout
  cannot save a buffered CI run anyway;
- events carry the port, so a listener is sweepable without `ready`;
- record the detached fixture's pid the moment Start-Process returns and
  tree-kill from it when readiness never arrives — previously that fixture
  had no teardown handle at all and outlived the run;
- document why the readiness deadline stays far below the 600s test cap.

* test(windows): unbind the ghost gate from the runtime it runs on

Three stalls, one commit, because they only separate under the runtime CI
uses (bun 1.4.x; the local default here is 1.3.6).

- The launch call never returned. execFileSync(powershell ...) with a stdout
  pipe waits for EOF, and the DETACHED fixture inherits that pipe, so it never
  closes while the fixture lives: the call returns only when something kills
  the fixture — which is why every red CI run showed the fixture alive for the
  full 600s and the ready line "after 0ms" (that is the moment the stall ended,
  not a handshake problem). The pid now travels through a file and the call
  runs with stdio 'ignore' — the same shape production's spawnDaemon() uses on
  Windows. Reproduced on bun 1.4.0 locally: the gate now proceeds.

- The scenario is runtime-dependent. bun >= 1.4 no longer inherits the
  listening socket into spawned children: identical code on one machine —
  1.3.6 leaves the port LISTENING under the dead worker, 1.4.0 releases it with
  the worker (the sidecar chain still survives; it just no longer holds the
  socket). Where no ghost forms and the chain was verified present, the gate
  now reports that and skips the recovery assertions instead of failing on the
  runtime's behaviour.

- Every child-process call in the gate is bounded now (taskkill had no
  timeout), and the kill-to-ghost window logs elapsed times, so a future stall
  names the step it is stuck in.

commits.commit_title: fix(windows): bound the port-occupancy probe so a ghost listener cannot hang the launcher (#3989)
commits.commit_message:
fix(windows): bound the port-occupancy probe so a ghost listener cannot hang the launcher (#3989)

isPortInUse()'s Windows fast path is an HTTP probe against /api/health, and it
was the one probe the ghost-listener reclaim (#3900) left unbounded. A ghost
listener — the dead worker's inherited socket, held open by its chroma sidecar
chain (#3603) — completes the TCP handshake and never answers, so the probe
never settled. ensureWorkerStarted() calls isPortInUse() BEFORE the reclaim, so
the reclaim could never run: instead of healing the ghost, every launcher
awaited a promise that never resolved. On CI that hung the gate added by #3900
for the full 600s test timeout in every run (12/12 red on main).

The probe now carries the same 5s abort budget as every other probe in the
module; on timeout the existing fall-through runs the socket probe, which still
reports a bound port as in use, so the launcher proceeds to the reclaim.

The gate gains stage lines and a 300s deadline around ensureWorkerStarted() so a
future unbounded await fails with a named error instead of a silent bun timeout.
Unit coverage pins the probe's abortable-signal contract and the fall-through.

* fix(observer): keep the claimed batch on a failed SDK turn

An error result carries no assistant text either, so forwarding the empty
response there acknowledged a batch the model never actually read. Gate
the forward on a successful, non-error result; failed turns leave the
claim intact for the next generator pass to re-yield.

* fix(observer): re-queue the batch a failed SDK turn never read

re-yields a claimed message, and the in-RAM buffer dies with the session,
so the batch was neither retried nor acknowledged. Reset it to pending so
the drain hands it to the next turn, once per generator pass — a batch
re-queued forever keeps a message pending, the buffer never idles out,
and a permanently failing turn would spin on it.

commits.commit_title: fix(observer): recognise the CLI's signed-out wording as an auth failure
commits.commit_message:
fix(observer): recognise the CLI's signed-out wording as an auth failure

* fix(observer): recognise the CLI's signed-out wording as an auth failure

Every pattern in isAuthFailureObserverOutput keys on the word 'authentication'.
The CLI does not use it when the profile is signed out - it prints 'Not logged
in - Please run /login' - so that response missed the auth branch, fell through
to the prose fallback, and was confirmed. Confirming a claimed batch discards
it: a reported fleet lost 857 batches over three hours with no observation
written and nothing to retry.

Two anchored patterns. The bare state must open the response, because an
observer narrating a past outage uses the same words, and the remediation half
must END it, so 'Please run /login in the observed project instructions' - an
existing must-not-match case - keeps running on into its sentence and stays
prose.

Refs #3606. Four matcher cases and one end-to-end case go red against main.

* fix(observer): the signed-out state must be the response, not open a sentence

An anchor is not a report test. A completed observation can open with the same
words - 'Not logged in during the reboot window; the observer recorded no new
findings' - and classifying it as an auth failure resets a batch that already
succeeded and pauses the generator.

The state now has to end the response, or introduce the rest with a separator,
which is what the CLI's own 'Not logged in - Please run /login' does. A trailing
full stop counts only when it ends there, so 'Not logged in. The observer
recorded...' stays prose.

Three narrative cases go red against the previous commit.

* fix(observer): anchor the signed-out status at both ends

A separator after the status is not a report test either: 'Not logged in - the
observer recorded nothing new' opens with the status, follows it with a
separator, and is a completed observation. A leading anchor answers prose that
runs on; it does not answer prose that runs on after punctuation.

Anchoring both ends closes it instead of narrowing it again. The CLI emits two
shapes and no third - the status alone, or the status plus its own /login
remediation - so both are matched exactly and nothing can trail them.

Three narrative cases go red against the previous commit.

commits.commit_title: fix(search): answer CJK and Japanese queries by substring
commits.commit_message:
fix(search): answer CJK and Japanese queries by substring

* fix(search): answer CJK and Japanese queries by substring

FTS5's unicode61 tokenizer has no delimiter to split Chinese or Japanese on,
so a whole run of ideographs folds into a single token. Every query in those
scripts is a substring of some longer run, and a substring of a token can
never match it -- so observation and session search returned 0 rows for any
multi-character CJK keyword, however many rows contained it.

Route queries containing an unsegmented script to a substring predicate over
the same columns the FTS table indexes. searchUserPrompts has always answered
this way, escaping included, so the semantics already exist in this class;
this extends them to the two tables that go through FTS.

Queries FTS5 can tokenize are untouched.

Fixes #3801

* fix(search): widen the unsegmented-script set to Bopomofo and Hangul

Review on #3810 pointed out two scripts sitting beside the ones this branch
already covered. Confirmed against tokenize='unicode61' rather than taken on
faith:

  설정   inside 설정을            -> 0 rows
  설정을 as a whole token         -> 1 row
  ㄓㄨ   inside ㄓㄨㄛ            -> 0 rows
  项目   inside 修改了项目配置    -> 0 rows   (the reported case)
  project inside "the project"    -> 1 row    (Latin, unaffected)

unicode61 breaks on Unicode whitespace and punctuation, and none of these
scripts put either between the characters of a run, so a run is one token and no
substring of it can match.

Korean is the interesting one: it does space its words, so only the sub-word
case is affected. That case is still every partial-word query a user types, and
the measurement above is exactly it.

The blocks are adjacent, so \u3100-\u318F picks up Bopomofo together with the
Hangul compatibility jamo beside it, and \uAC00-\uD7AF covers the syllables.

Two tests, one per script. Narrowing the class back to the previous ranges fails
both.

commits.commit_title: fix(server-beta): accept contentSessionId on /v1/memories, mirroring /v1/events
commits.commit_message:
fix(server-beta): accept contentSessionId on /v1/memories, mirroring /v1/events

* fix(server-beta): accept contentSessionId on /v1/memories, mirroring /v1/events

#2634 taught the ingest path to resolve contentSessionId into a server_sessions
row, because callers writing from inside a session know the agent's own session
id, not the server_sessions row UUID. The memory write path never got the same
affordance: /v1/memories accepts only serverSessionId.

Any client writing a memory from within a session therefore lands with
server_session_id NULL, and those rows can never be grouped, scoped or compared
by session afterwards. Measured on a production deployment: 2,948 of 2,948 such
observations (100%) are unlinked, against 85.7% linked on rows produced through
the generation path.

Accept contentSessionId and resolve it the same way. An explicit serverSessionId
still wins; the lookup is best-effort and a failure stores the memory unlinked
exactly as before, so no write can start failing because of this.

Unlike /v1/events there is no idempotency concern: observations key off id and
server_session_id is a plain FK (ON DELETE SET NULL), so resolving the link later
cannot drift a key -- the drift raised in review of #2634 does not apply here.

Tests: 4 cases in the #2634 linkage suite -- explicit id wins without querying,
contentSessionId resolves, neither id stores unlinked, and a throwing lookup
never fails the write.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(server-beta): scope memory linkage by platform and thread it through the client

Addresses both review findings.

1. Platform scope was lost (greptile P1 / codex P2). resolveMemorySessionLink
   called findIdByContentSessionId without the platform scope, so when two
   sessions in the same team/project share a contentSessionId the lookup fell
   back to whichever started last -- a Cursor memory could be attached to a
   Codex session. The route now accepts platformSource and passes the scope
   through the same sessionLookupPlatformScope helper the ingest path uses, so
   an omitted field and an explicit null keep meaning different things.

2. No supported caller could send the field (codex P2). The route accepted
   contentSessionId but ServerAddObservationRequest, buildAddObservationPayload
   and the MCP observation_add args exposed only serverSessionId, so in-repo
   callers kept producing unlinked memories. All three now carry
   contentSessionId and platformSource.

Tests: two cases pinning the scope -- the platform reaches the query, and an
omitted platformSource is distinguishable from an explicit null.

commits.commit_title: fix(server-beta): re-pin payload.generation_job_id on idempotent re-create
commits.commit_message:
fix(server-beta): re-pin payload.generation_job_id on idempotent re-create

A generation job whose payload points at a non-existent job id is dropped
silently: `ProviderObservationGenerator` resolves the row through
`payload.generation_job_id`, so `lockOutbox` finds nothing, logs at info level
and returns `{ status: "completed" }` to BullMQ without ever touching Postgres.
The queue reports success, the row stays `queued` forever, and nothing is
recorded as failed.

That pointer goes stale on the upsert path. Every re-create mints a fresh id
for `$1` and puts the same id in the payload it hands over. On
`ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key)` the existing row wins, so the minted id is
discarded for the `id` column -- but `payload || excluded.payload` still lets
it overwrite `generation_job_id`, leaving the row pointing at an id that was
never inserted.

This only bites `session_summary`. Its idempotency key is derived from
`sourceId`, which for summaries is the session, so every re-run of a session
summary collides. Event jobs key off the individual event id and never conflict.

Re-pin `generation_job_id` to the surviving row inside the same merge.

Notes for reviewers:
- An operator re-queue flow that "reuses the persisted payload" (#2459 /
  discussion #2460) does not recover these rows: replaying the stored payload
  replays the stale pointer, and the job is dropped again just as silently.
- Observed on a production deployment running server-beta since May: 190 summary
  jobs stranded in `queued` across four months, 190/190 with
  `payload->>generation_job_id` absent from the table. Event jobs on the same
  instance: 0 divergences in ~221k rows. After re-pointing the payload the same
  rows started draining immediately.

Co-authored-by: Alessandro <alessandropcostabr@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.commit_title: fix: say why the worker died instead of listing suspects (#3894)
commits.commit_message:
fix: say why the worker died instead of listing suspects (#3894)

A worker that dies during module resolution left nothing behind. spawnDaemon
detaches it with its stdio discarded — Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden on
Windows, stdio:'ignore' elsewhere — so the only trace was "Worker exited before
readiness endpoint became available", followed by a guess-list of Bun, the
bundle and the port. None of those was the cause when this last happened: a
truncated `bun install` in the plugin cache had left zod short 37 files, and
every claude-mem hook failed for hours with nothing in the log to say so.

Probe the bundle on the failure path and log what it actually says. `status` is
the probe command because it executes every top-level require — where these
failures happen, long before argv is parsed — then exits 0 without starting a
server, so a healthy bundle costs one silent subprocess. The reason also rides
out through getLastWorkerBootFailure() into the `start` hook's status line,
which is the one place a user reliably looks.

The probe needs a retry to work at all where it matters most: called from the
failure path under Bun 1.3.13 on Windows, the first sync spawn returns
ETIMEDOUT in ~25ms with the child SIGTERMed before printing a byte, identically
at an 8s and a 60s timeout, while a second identical spawn answers in ~180ms.
shouldRetryWorkerBootProbe gates that retry on a window that expired far too
early to be real, so a genuine timeout — the bundle loaded and kept running —
is still never retried.

startSession sends the briefing prompt as a standalone query and hands
its reply straight to the storage path, so a model that answers the
brief with a well-formed <observation> gets it stored as memory. The
brief cannot legitimately contain one: buildInitPrompt shows the output
format alongside an <observed_from_primary_session> block holding only
<user_request> and <requested_at>, with no tool call and nothing
observed. What lands is a paraphrase of the user's prompt, asserting
work that has not happened, and it then feeds cross-session context
injection like any real observation.

Measured on a non-Anthropic provider: 2 of 12 sessions. `files_modified:
[]` is the fingerprint, since sanitizeObservationFiles strips file
claims no claimed message supports and at init there are none.

handleInitResponse now keeps the reply's token accounting and appends it
as the assistant turn itself rather than routing it through
processAgentResponse. Role alternation is unchanged; only the storage
call goes away. session.lastUsage is deliberately no longer set here —
ResponseProcessor reads and nulls it, so with no consumer on this path
it leaked the init call's usage into the next observation's telemetry.

Not fixed here: ClaudeProvider is exposed the same way, but the SDK
streams, so a fix there turns on the one-reply-per-turn invariant rather
than a return value and deserves its own change.

The two gemini_provider tests that stored through the init query are
re-targeted at a tool call; they were exercising the store pipeline, not
asserting that a brief reply is memory.

commits.commit_title: fix(hooks): dedupe file-context injection per session (#3480)
commits.commit_message:
fix(hooks): dedupe file-context injection per session (#3480)

* fix(hooks): dedupe file-context injection per session (#3480)

The PreToolUse file-context handler re-injected the same "prior
observations" timeline on every Read/Grep of an unchanged file within a
session — the only gate was file-mtime staleness, with no per-(session,
file) memoization. Repeatedly reading the same file (iterative debugging,
long sessions) multiplied context cost with zero new information.

Add a small persistent per-session store (one JSON file per session under
DATA_DIR/file-context-seen) keyed by resolved file path → newest injected
observation epoch. A repeated unchanged Read is now skipped; re-injection
happens only when a newer observation has been recorded since. In-memory
memoization is impossible here because each hook runs in a freshly spawned
process. Stale session files are pruned (7-day TTL) on a session's first
write so the store stays bounded.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): make file-context dedupe keys collision-free (#3480)

Address two P1 review findings on the per-session file-context dedupe store:

- Session-id store filenames: replace the non-injective char-replace scheme
  (`[^A-Za-z0-9_-] -> _`) with a sha256 hex digest of the complete session id.
  `a.b` and `a:b` no longer collapse to the same `a_b.json` and cross-suppress
  each other's initial injection. Still path-safe and traversal-proof.

- Dedupe path key: normalize with `path.resolve(cwd, filePath)` for absolute
  inputs too, so dot-segment aliases (`/p/src/../src/f.ts` vs `/p/src/f.ts`)
  collapse to one canonical key instead of double-injecting the same file.

RED -> GREEN: two new regression tests in tests/hooks/file-context.test.ts fail
on the pre-fix code (collision suppresses the distinct session; alias bypasses
dedupe) and pass after. Full file-context suite 17 pass; typecheck clean; full
`bun test tests` baseline unchanged (27 pre-existing failures before and after,
+2 new passing tests).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): order file-context store setup before prune check (#3486)

* fix(hooks): persist the file-context gate in SQLite, not a JSON side-store (#3480)

Review feedback on #3486 asked for plan-20 (#3608) step 4: the file-context
injection gate must be a row in the main database keyed per (session, file,
observation epoch), not a JSON file under DATA_DIR.

What changed:

- The gate moves from one JSON file per session under `file-context-seen/` to
  a `file_context_injections` table in `claude-mem.db`. The table is device-
  local: sync enumerates the tables it pushes explicitly, and this is not one.
- `wasFileContextInjected` + `recordFileContextInjection` collapse into a
  single `claimFileContextInjection`. Claiming IS recording, in one
  `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... RETURNING` statement, so two concurrent Reads of
  the same file in one session can no longer both inject — the read-before-write
  race the previous store shipped with (and documented as acceptable) is gone.
- The upsert guard `excluded.observation_epoch > stored` keeps the stored epoch
  monotonic, so a hook that finishes late carrying an older epoch neither wins
  the claim nor rolls the row back to a stale value.
- The claim moved to the very end of `buildFileContextTimeline`, after every
  other reason to bail out, so a suppressed injection never burns the claim.
- `resolveDbPath()` resolves the database path at call time. `DB_PATH` freezes
  `DATA_DIR` at import, which is right for the long-lived worker but wrong for
  a per-invocation hook process that must honour a `CLAUDE_MEM_DATA_DIR` set
  after the module loaded (and is what lets the tests point at a temp dir).

Failing open is preserved: an unopenable database or a failed claim injects
rather than throwing, which is never worse than the un-deduped behaviour.

commits.commit_title: fix(daemon): accept a clarification turn whose Runtime State names the wrong stage (#7980)
commits.commit_message:
fix(daemon): accept a clarification turn whose Runtime State names the wrong stage (#7980)

After the user answers the one clarification round, the agent's next turn
carries a complete Full Plan plus a Runtime State. On 0.22.1-prerelease.9
(OPEND-2954) that state said `inputStage: "request"` — the value every
Runtime State example in the protocol reference shows, and the one field the
clarification continuation never named — and the coordinator refused the turn
on that field alone. The task settled terminal-`blocked`, a plan that passed
every other gate never reached production, and no repair path could anchor on
it because the block was schema-valid and the mismatch is not a parser issue.

The stage is host-owned truth: the daemon issued it, wrote it into the
continuation wrapper, and holds it on the task, so a disagreeing declaration
carries no authority — the same footing as the execution mode a clarification
turn predicts, which the parser already discards. `adoptHostInputStage` now
gives the state the host's stage before validation whenever the corrected
state is a valid declaration for that stage, and records the decision as a
normalization rather than a reason code so an agent-declared `blocked` keeps
its own attribution. Where the field does carry meaning — a second
`clarification_required`, a `plan_ready` at production — the corrected state
fails the contract, the agent's value stands, and the turn is refused exactly
as before. The serialization-repair anchor gets the same treatment so a fenced
plan on a clarification turn can still enter its one repair.

The clarification continuation now also says which stage it runs at, mirroring
the production continuation's `inputStage production`, so the agent has one
sentence to follow instead of three examples that all say `request`.

Specs: a clarification turn declaring `request` / `plan_ready` with a valid
plan reaches `plan_ready` (red on main: blocked with
`od_next_protocol_stage_mismatch`); an agent-declared block with the wrong
stage keeps `od_next_agent_declared_block`; a second question round is still
refused; a fenced plan with the wrong stage still anchors a repair; the
continuation text names `inputStage clarification`.

Co-authored-by: Cheems <216108319+hihicheems@users.noreply.github.com>

commits.commit_title: fix(daemon): keep proxy Basic credentials off the media wait tool-token lane (#8006)
commits.commit_message:
fix(daemon): keep proxy Basic credentials off the media wait tool-token lane (#8006)

* fix(daemon): keep proxy Basic credentials off the media wait tool-token lane

The media task wait route selected the run-scoped tool-token lane on the
mere presence of an Authorization header. Tool tokens are only ever
parsed out of a Bearer header (bearerTokenFromRequest), so a reverse
proxy that authenticates browsers itself and forwards its own
`Authorization: Basic ...` could never satisfy that lane: every proxied
poll of POST /api/media/tasks/:id/wait failed 401 TOOL_TOKEN_MISSING,
so image and video generation never reported completion.

Gate the lane on the Bearer scheme. The existing intent is preserved —
once a Bearer caller does choose the lane, invalid, expired or
under-scoped credentials still must not downgrade to project
authorization; this only changes what counts as choosing it.

The other two authorizeToolRequest callers in this file,
/api/tools/media/scaffold and /api/tools/media/generate, are agent-only
endpoints that unconditionally require a tool token and are unchanged.

Same root cause as #7819, which covers the export and archive routes in
apps/daemon/src/import-export-routes.ts.

* fix(daemon): fail closed on a malformed Bearer credential

Review catch: `authorizationHeader.trim()` reduces `Authorization: Bearer `
to `Bearer`, which the `/^Bearer\s+/i` predicate rejected. That sent a
malformed Bearer credential to `authorizeProjectRequest` instead of
`authorizeToolRequest`, so a caller reaching for the tool-token lane could
reach the browser project-authority lane — before this branch, any
Authorization header produced TOOL_TOKEN_MISSING.

Classify the scheme independently of whether a token follows it, so both
`Bearer` and `Bearer <invalid>` stay on the tool-token lane and fail closed,
while Basic credentials still reach project authorization.

Regression coverage added for `Bearer ` and a bare `Bearer`; both return a
full task snapshot (HTTP 200) with the previous predicate and 401 with this
one.

commits.commit_title: fix(daemon,web): stop a delivered OD Next turn reporting as failed, and name the real gate (#7931)
commits.commit_message:
fix(daemon,web): stop a delivered OD Next turn reporting as failed, and name the real gate (#7931)

* fix(daemon,web): stop a refused turn reporting a delivered deck as failed

One predicate answered two different questions, and the strict answer is the
wrong answer to the loose one.

`validateRunDeliverable` asks "did THIS run write the canonical entry". That is
the right gate for accepting an Agent's completion claim — a turn must not pass
by pointing at a file an earlier turn wrote. It is also `false` for the most
ordinary shape of an OD Next refusal: the user types 「继续」, the agent
re-checks work an earlier turn already finished, correctly rewrites nothing,
and the turn is refused over its machine block.

Both safety nets read that one answer, so both went down together. The
coordinator's completion inference declined, and `deliveredDespiteBlock` in the
web provider — the carve-out that exists to keep a delivered turn out of the
failure branch — could never fire. A field report shows the result: a red
「回复已收到,但没能记录下来」card under a finished 16-page deck the user could
see rendered in the preview pane beside it. The physical run had exited 0 and
the 2.27 MB file was on disk.

`validateProjectDeliverable` is the second question: does the user have it,
right now. Same entry resolution, same kind contract, same readability check,
minus the run-scoped gates. `GET /api/runs/:id` resolves it only for a terminal
run whose strategy task settled blocked — the one case a client has to
distinguish — and logs the answer, because withholding a failure the user
cannot act on is right and withholding it invisibly is not.

The verdict does not move: the task still blocks, the strategy contract still
refuses to complete on an unproven claim, and a turn that delivered nothing
still fails with its card. What changes is that a bookkeeping failure no longer
tells a user they lost work that is sitting in their project.

This is also what `docs/design/run-errors/error-ux-design.md` §3 already ruled
for the case: 「文件生成了但进程报错:算成功」, with the stated reason that doing
otherwise "把一堆无害报错变成失败潮".

Red spec: apps/web/tests/providers/strategy-blocked-verdict.test.ts
「does not become a failure when the project holds the deliverable」 — red on
main, green here.

* fix(daemon,web): name the gate that refused a turn, not the parser that noticed

The protocol parser raises `od_next_protocol_runtime_state_missing` before
`validateAcceptedTurn` — the function that owns the real gates — is ever
reached. So every block-less turn was filed under the parser's own code, and
`reasonCodes[0]` is what the failure card, the diagnostics export and the
analytics bucket all read.

The effect on a user who got nothing this round: they were told a marker was
missing. True of the reply, useless to them, and not the reason the turn could
not succeed — the identical failure with a DECLARED block reported
`od_next_canonical_deliverable_invalid`, the host fact they can act on. Two
names for one failure, and the less useful one was the one that shipped.

`reattributeUndeclaredTurn` already existed for exactly this, scoped to one
cell (a clarification turn that asked again). Extend it: when a block-less turn
was SHAPED like a completion the host may infer and the inference still
declined, the evidence is what refused — both helpers gate on the shape, which
just held, and the evidence. Lead with it. The parser's code stays behind it,
because `blocked_reason_codes_json` is the durable record of what the turn
actually wrote, and a triage that cannot tell "declared badly" from "declared
nothing" has lost the one distinction that decides whether a serialization
repair was ever possible.

ATTRIBUTION ONLY — no verdict moves. The two existing specs that pinned the old
name still assert the verdict they own and now assert the new attribution; the
turns they describe block exactly as before.

`od_next_canonical_deliverable_invalid` gets the card it now needs. It is
deliberately not the Runtime State copy: those say "your reply went missing",
this says "nothing came out this round", and only the second is true when the
project is empty. Retry earns its place here — the deliverable is missing
because this turn wrote nothing, and a re-run is the thing that can write it.

⚠️ The copy is engineering's, like the rows around it. `error-ux-design.md` has
no cell for it; S23 (跑完没生成文件) is the nearest and is listed there as
invisible in telemetry. Product should rewrite the wording, not the routing.

Red spec: apps/daemon/tests/strategies/od-next/coordinator.test.ts
「names the evidence that refused an undeclared completion, not the parser」 and
「gives the undeclared and declared shapes of one failure the same name」 — both
red on main, green here.

* feat(daemon): make an OD Next block countable instead of invisible

`run_finished.result` is derived from the physical run status
(`runResultFromStatus`: `succeeded → success`), and a refused OD Next turn
normally exits 0 with a complete reply on screen. So this entire class of
failure reported `result: 'success'` while the user was looking at a red card,
and nothing queryable disagreed — the reason codes lived only in the task
store's `blocked_reason_codes_json` and in a client-side error object.

`error-ux-design.md` §《线上频次与优先级》 already flags the shape of this
problem for S23/S24: 「被算成了成功 —— 看不到是坏事:线上到底有多少,我们不知
道」. OD Next made it worse than invisible by pairing the silent metric with a
visible failure card.

Carrying `reasonCodes[0]` — the same value the card keys on — makes the class
countable without changing what `result` means. Read off the run's own terminal
projection, the object the SSE `end` payload and the failure card were both
built from, so the three cannot drift. Omitted for every run whose strategy
task did not block, which is the common case.

This is the half that makes the suppression in the preceding commits safe to
ship: a failure the user is no longer shown is one we can still count.

* fix(web): do not go silent on a turn that produced no reply either

The preceding fix credits a deliverable an EARLIER turn wrote, which is right
for the case it was written for — the agent re-checks finished work and
correctly rewrites nothing — and wrong for the mirror case in #7564: a blank OD
Next response into a project that already holds a prototype. There the file is
real and the user still got nothing, so withholding the card swaps one wrong
answer for the other.

Require the turn to have actually said something before the looser field can
suppress a failure. The accumulated assistant text is already on hand in the
stream consumer, so this costs nothing and needs no new daemon field.

The stricter field keeps its existing behaviour untouched: an artifact THIS run
produced is delivery whether or not the agent narrated it.

Red spec: apps/web/tests/providers/strategy-blocked-verdict.test.ts
「still fails when the turn produced no reply at all」 — verified red with the
guard removed, green with it.

* refactor(contracts): make the OD Next block dimension a tested pure mapper

Observability that nothing exercises is observability that rots. The derivation
was inline in the run lifecycle, where the only way to reach it is to boot the
whole analytics flow — so it would have failed silently to "field absent",
which is indistinguishable from "no run ever blocked".

Move it next to `harnessAnalyticsFromRolloutDecision`, which answers the
neighbouring question about the same run and already has a suite. The edges
that matter are the ones a wrong answer would quietly mislabel: a task that has
not settled, one that settled on something other than `blocked`, and a blocked
one an older daemon projected without a reason.

commits.commit_message:
fix(prompts): write next-step suggestions in the run's UI locale (#7920)

The three follow-up suggestions under a completed turn are written by the
model, not picked from i18n files, so the only thing that decides their
language is the prompt. That prompt carried one soft rule — "write them in
the language the user is speaking" — printed directly under three English
examples, and nothing about the run's actual locale.

The locale rule lived only in `# UI locale override`, a section of the
cache-stable prompt head that `server.ts` deliberately drops on resume turns
to protect the upstream prompt cache. The keyed follow-up block is re-sent
every turn. So the rule was absent exactly on the turns that carry the
marker, and a zh-CN run closed with English suggestions — one of them a
near-copy of the prompt's own example.

Thread the run locale into `renderChatTurnHostProtocolInstructions` so the
per-turn block states its own language requirement, including the existing
brand/code/technical-identifier exception so `localStorage` and `CTA` still
survive. An English or absent locale renders byte-for-byte what it did
before. Also collapses the third copy of the zh-CN/zh-TW name mapping into
`prompts/ui-locale.ts`.

commits.commit_title: fix(chat): keep each folded run's own clock (#7921)
commits.commit_message:
fix(chat): keep each folded run's own clock (#7921)

* fix(chat): keep each folded run's own clock

A logical OD Next task runs as several physical Runs, and reopening a
conversation folds them into one turn. The fold keeps one message row, so
only Run 0's createdAt and Run N's endedAt survive and every Run boundary
in between is discarded. The renderer is then left with one clock for N
Runs, which shows up as two separate reports:

  - a Run's shell with no timestamped events of its own (clarification
    Runs typically have none, and the plain-stream agent family never
    emits any) reaches neither the "opened this round" nor the "closed
    this round" fallback, so its head is a bare "Done" with no duration;
  - a thinking gap, inferred from "last timestamped event until the next
    one", runs straight across the Run boundary and charges earlier Runs'
    wall-clock time - including the minutes the user spent answering a
    question form - to the current Run's Thoughts row, which then reports
    more than the card head containing it.

Both are reload-only: strategyTaskRunIndex is served by the history
endpoint alone, so the same conversation renders correctly while live and
loses the numbers once reopened.

Restore the lost boundary rather than adjust either number. The fold
stamps each Run's own span onto the done_key it already emits, and the
renderer scopes the shell clock and the thinking gap to that Run. On the
recorded three-Run conversation the reloaded turn now reports 1m 20s /
2m 39s / 4m 42s and a 2m 57s Thoughts row - identical, to the millisecond,
to what the same Runs report live.

Also make a card's span cover the thinking row it credits, so the same
invariant holds for a second card opened mid-Run after a done marker.

OPEND-2823, OPEND-2824

* fix(chat): stop a card borrowing another run's clock

Review of #7921 caught the other half of the same defect. shellElapsed
still seeded from/to from the turn-global firstStartedAt/lastEndedAt when
a shell had no shellSpan of its own, then unioned those leftovers with the
new per-run bounds. A folded successor run that emits only status and text
- the typical clarification run, and every plain-stream agent - has no
shellSpan, so its card picked up the preceding run's tool timestamps and
reported that run's time as its own.

So the first commit fixed "a middle run shows no number" but left "the
number belongs to another run", behind a different trigger.

Drop the turn-global seed instead of clearing those clocks in closeRun().
firstStartedAt/lastEndedAt are the min/max of every timestamp in the turn,
so when this shell has no span of its own any value there was necessarily
stamped by a different shell: the fallback is, by construction, always
borrowing another card's clock and can never once be this card's own time.
Clearing at the run boundary would also only cover the cross-run trigger -
the identical borrow happens inside a single run when a second card opens
after a done marker with no timestamped events, where closeRun() never
runs - and it would silently change thinkGapStart and shellQuiet, which
read the same two clocks.

On the review's shape a card that ran for 20s reported 5m 10s; it now
reports 20s, which is what the same run reports live.

OPEND-2823, OPEND-2824

* docs(contracts): clarify missing folded-run timing boundaries

commits.commit_title: feat(web): wire up the ChatPanel observability that was never called (#7930)
commits.commit_message:
feat(web): wire up the ChatPanel observability that was never called (#7930)

* feat(web): make chat telemetry name the run it is talking about

`setChatCorrelation()` has had no production caller since #7518. Every
`client_chat_*` event therefore shipped with an empty correlation block, and
`client_chat_interaction_latency` — the one chat observability event with real
traffic (2,694 events / 30 days) — derives its `streaming` flag from
`chatCorrelation().run_id`. With no producer the flag was false on every event
ever sent, so the panel read "every chat stall happens while the app sits
idle": a self-consistent, wrong story, and the reason the metric was worse
than no metric.

Wire the four producers that already had their values in hand:

- run id + agent id, opened at every run start (`streamViaDaemon`, the next
  physical run of a strategy-task chain, and `reattachDaemonRun` — the path a
  page refresh takes back onto a run still in flight) and closed in the same
  `finally` that settles the stuck-run watchdog. Named helpers, because the
  pair is load-bearing: only an opener and `streaming` is stuck true forever;
  only a closer and it is stuck false.
- conversation id + project id, once `listMessages` resolves.
- release channel, off `/api/version` — the daemon has always answered with
  `channel` and the web read `version` and dropped the rest.
- replay session id, handed over from the posthog-js instance inside
  `loaded()`. This is the only possible source: the ESM build never publishes
  itself as `window.posthog`, so the global-lookup fallback returns undefined
  forever while looking implemented.

No new events. This only makes the traffic already being sent tell the truth.

`model_id` stays absent — it is not in scope at either run-start site, and a
guess would be worse than the gap.

* feat(analytics): record which failure sentence the user actually read

`run_failed_toast` says a user was shown a failure card and names the daemon's
`error_code`. It cannot say what the user READ — those two facts are separated
by a mapping table, and `resolveRunErrorCardDescription` states in as many
words that the table can always be one row short. When it is, the card falls
back to a blank "the task failed" with no diagnosis. That is the worst
impression this surface produces, and it was the one we could not count.

Add two fields to the exposure:

- `message_key` — the i18n key of the mapped copy, or `generic_fallback` when
  the table had no line for it. Always present, never omitted: the fallback
  RATE is the number that matters, and a rate needs a denominator, so an
  omitted key would drop the fallback impressions out of the very count meant
  to measure them.
- `failure_category` — the daemon's own classification off the run's error
  event, defaulting to the enum's existing `unknown` member rather than
  vanishing, so this event stays joinable against `run_finished` and
  `run_recovery_action`.

`message_key` is typed as `string`, not the web's `RunFailureMessageKey`
union: that union lives in apps/web and grows with every copy change, and
pinning it in contracts would make adding a sentence a contracts change.

* feat(web): attach the chat-health monitor to the chat log

`chat-health.ts` has answered four questions since #7518 — how long until the
user can read the conversation, is the DOM growing without bound, who is about
to OOM, how janky is the UI while a run streams — and nothing but its own unit
spec has ever called it. All four tiles were empty in production.

Open a surface on the `.chat-log` element while the Chat tab is showing it,
and tear it down when it goes away. Two effect dependencies, each guarding a
real failure:

- `tab`, because the log is conditionally rendered and `logRef.current` is
  null on the Comments tab — without it, coming back to Chat never reattaches.
- `activeConversationId`, because that div carries no conversation key, so
  React reuses the very same DOM node across a switch. There is no node-level
  signal that the surface should be replaced; the id is the only one. The
  spec pins this by asserting node identity is unchanged AND that a second
  surface opened anyway.

`markFirstPaint` lands together with `setStreamEventCount`, deliberately: a
first-paint duration on its own cannot be attributed, because a slow open is
either "many messages" or "one message with hundreds of tool events behind
it", and only the event count separates them. Rendered-row count uses the same
`:scope > *` definition `client_chat_dom_growth` already uses, so the two
events are comparable.

Run start / end feed the jank window from the daemon provider, which is where
the authoritative run lifecycle lives. Both no-op when no chat surface is
mounted.

Also extracts `isChatVirtualized()` so the renderer and the telemetry read the
same predicate. Two copies of `items.length > THRESHOLD` are identical today
and drift the first time the rule grows a second term — at which point the
telemetry would describe a render mode the renderer no longer uses, silently.

`markChatOpenIntent` is NOT wired here. Hanging it off the two conversation
handlers would only cover `conversation_switch`; `project_switch` has 10+
navigate sites in App.tsx and `cold_boot` passes through no handler at all.
The right home is `router.ts`, which is the single navigation entry point and
can derive the open kind from the route transition. That is its own change.
Until then `open_kind` honestly reads `remount` rather than a fabricated
`cold_boot`.

* fix(web): stop the wiring from reintroducing the bug it removes

Three review findings, all real, all the same family: an event that cannot
name what it measured.

1. `client_chat_stream_health` was going out with an empty `run_id`.
   `chatSurfaceRunEnded()` does not merely bookkeep — it FLUSHES the jank
   window, and the flush spreads `chatCorrelation()`. The terminal path
   cleared the correlation one line earlier, so the one event this PR newly
   enables shipped anonymous: the exact defect the PR exists to remove,
   reintroduced by the fix for it.

   One rule now covers both ends of a run: the chat-health call goes FIRST,
   because it is the one that can emit; the correlation mutation goes second.
   Applied symmetrically at the three run-start sites too — `runStarted()`
   flushes any window a previous run left open (its terminal event never
   arrived), and that flush belongs to the OLD run, so it has to happen before
   the block is repointed. `trackRunTerminal` is unaffected either way; it
   carries its own context and never reads this block.

2. A surface opened mid-run did not know a run was running. Surfaces are
   recreated on every conversation switch and every return to the Chat tab,
   but `chatSurfaceRunStarted` only ever reached the surface that existed when
   the provider fired it. The new surface kept its window shut and dropped
   every long task until the next run start — precisely the stretch a user is
   watching, because they came back to the tab to see something generate.

   `openChatSurface` now adopts the in-flight run. It reads it from the
   correlation context rather than keeping a second flag: `chat-interaction.ts`
   already derives its `streaming` breakdown the same way, and one source
   cannot disagree with itself. No double counting — `runCount` and the window
   clock are per-surface, and adoption only ever runs against the surface
   constructed a line above it. The spec pins this with three long tasks split
   across a mid-run swap and asserts they add up to three, not four.

3. `conversation_id` / `project_id` moved from ProjectView to the ChatPane
   boundary. ChatPane has three hosts — ProjectView, DesignSystemFlow and
   workspace/SideChatTab — feeding one set of observability modules and one
   dashboard. Setting it in a single host left the other two emitting orphan
   rows indistinguishable from genuinely un-correlated ones. Both already pass
   the ids in as props. The effect is declared ahead of the surface-open effect
   so the opening `conversation_open` sample is already stamped.

commits.commit_title: fix(chat): make the run-failure card's retry tell the truth about the send gate (#7927)
commits.commit_message:
fix(chat): make the run-failure card's retry tell the truth about the send gate (#7927)

* fix(chat): make the run-failure card's retry tell the truth about the send gate

Three reports that all land on the same gate in ProjectView:
`currentConversationActionDisabled`, which every recovery handler consults
and no button was ever wired to.

OPEND-2821 — the retry button had no `disabled` at all, so it always looked
live. Clicking it reported a `manual_retry` recovery click and then
`handleRetry` returned. Split that boolean into a four-way reason
(read-only / messages-unavailable / billing-unresolved / conversation-busy),
disable the card's recovery actions when it is set, and say which one it is.
The split is a partition of the same predicate, proven exhaustively.

OPEND-2758 — `handleSend` paints the new turn before the preflight and before
POST /api/runs (OPEND-2614, deliberate), and that paint makes
`retryableAssistantMessage` return null, so the card vanished 1-2s before
anything was confirmed. Announce the pending retry, pin the card on the
message being retried, lock the button and label it "Retrying", and drop the
announcement only when the replacement message gets its run id -- or when the
send never started, which restores the original card and its actions.

OPEND-2719 — an exhausted wallet parked the send in the pending-send queue.
The queue means "this runs once capacity frees up"; an empty wallet never
frees up, so the message sat there forever. Stop queueing that one branch
(`signed_out` keeps its queue-and-resume path) and hand the draft back to the
composer through the existing `restore-draft` outcome. The report's other
half did not reproduce: the dialog and balance card were already re-firing on
every blocked send.

Note on telemetry: a blocked click no longer counts as a recovery click. It
never produced a run to join against, so those were unjoinable orphans; the
existing surface_view still records that the action was offered.

* fix(chat): claim the composer draft positively instead of by exclusion

Review on #7927: the no-queue path for an exhausted wallet used an
exclusion predicate — "not a retry and not a queue drain, therefore the
composer owns it". ProjectView has eleven other direct `handleSend`
callers (share to community, design-system feedback and review decisions,
continue remaining tasks, resume run, question-form answers, Home
auto-send, resend-failed-user-message, brand extraction and enrichment,
the auto-audit repair effect, Antigravity OAuth repair). None of them
holds its payload in the composer, and all of them were being swept onto
that path — which silently took away their queue. The question-form
answer is the worst case: it keeps the only copy of the answer and its
uploads, and releases the form only on a durable-queue acknowledgement.

Replace it with an explicit `composerOwnedDraft` marker that only
`handleComposerSend` sets. Everything else falls through to the queueing
path it had before this branch, unchanged. The marker is transport-only
and is stripped alongside `acceptDurableQueue` before queue persistence:
once a send is parked, the queue item owns the payload, not the composer.

commits.commit_title: fix(daemon): let a failed media generation reach its run terminal (#7933)
commits.commit_message:
fix(daemon): let a failed media generation reach its run terminal (#7933)

A turn whose only deliverable failed reported "Completed" with a green
check. The daemon knew better: it logged `[media] {"event":"failed",
"run_id":…,"status":400}` and shipped the same run id to analytics, then
told the run nothing. Two halves of one invariant:

- routes/media.ts never wrote the failure back. `runId` was already in
  `options.grant`; both failure paths (the provider rejection and the
  synchronous dispatch throw) marked the task failed, emitted analytics,
  logged, and returned. The run's verdict was left to the child's exit
  code, and the agent exits 0 after apologising in prose.

- the turn-completion marker vetoed "unfinished" on nothing but "marker
  matches the run's key, and some non-empty text follows it". In the
  reported run that following text was the S22 apology we ask the model
  to copy verbatim — so the apology suppressed the very signal it was
  apologising for, over a TodoWrite snapshot that had a `cancelled` item.

`noteMediaTaskFailure` is the dual of `associateLateRunProducedFile`:
one hands the turn the bytes a 202 dispatch produced, the other hands it
the fact that it produced none. The terminal derivation reads that
host-recorded fact as its own term, outside the marker/strategy/todo
clause, so the model's account of its own turn cannot overrule a failure
the host watched happen. The evidence is never the agent's words: the
apology is product copy and may be rewritten at any time.

Scoped to the attempt (`prepareRestart` clears it) and gated on
`succeeded`, so a user-canceled turn and a turn holding no host
counter-evidence keep exactly the verdict they have today.

commits.commit_title: feat(release): post the prerelease card on trigger and time every platform (#7916)
commits.commit_message:
feat(release): post the prerelease card on trigger and time every platform (#7916)

Reverses the "withhold the card until the first artifact publishes" rule.
The card is now posted on the watcher's first poll, while every platform is
still queued, and every later state edits that same message.

The reason the card was withheld — a "构建中…" message left standing forever
when a build dies — has since been answered by the machinery that grew around
the card: a dead lane renders its own terminal state, a release where nothing
shipped turns the card red, the watcher's 140-minute budget stamps the card
instead of abandoning it, and a watcher that never delivered draws the
fallback bot. Silence for the whole build window bought nothing.

`shouldPostFirstCard` conflated two predicates. One half was already
`anyPackagePublished`; the other is now `allPlatformsFailed`, and it moves
from gating the post to being the card's red verdict — the header's old
"some platform reported and none shipped" proxy is only equivalent while the
card does not exist before total failure, and with the card posted early it
reads 全部平台构建失败 the moment one lane fails, or red at t=0 because
`build_linux` is skipped on every run.

Each platform row now carries its build time (`用时 11m42s` once finished,
`已用 18m` while running) and the footer carries the whole round's clock, both
read from the `started_at` / `completed_at` already in the polled job list
plus the origin run's `created_at`. Live numbers are quantized to the minute
so a 30-second poll does not PATCH the card on every cycle.
