commits.commit_title: feat(daemon): make OD Next the default route, and keep the switch usable (#7876)
commits.commit_message:
feat(daemon): make OD Next the default route, and keep the switch usable (#7876)

* feat(daemon): make OD Next the default route, and keep an opt-out opted out

An installation that configured nothing ran the ordinary strategy route, so
shipping OD Next in a build never changed how a run behaved until someone
opened Settings and asked for it. That made the Labs switch the whole rollout:
the strategy could only reach the users who already knew to look for it.

`resolveRequestedMode` now resolves an unconfigured installation to `active`.
Every other admission condition already defaulted open — assignment bucket,
both content flags, the production approval flag — so this last default was the
only thing holding the route closed.

The one-line change is the small part. Flipping the default inverts which case
is load-bearing. While the strategy was opt-in, an installation that lost its
saved mode kept the behaviour it already had; now an installation that loses
its saved mode is switched back on. So the invariant this has to keep is that
an installation which opted out reads `off` through every later release, and
that rests on opting out being stored rather than erased: `off` is a value the
config carries, `applyConfigValue` drops the key only for a value it cannot
store, and `assertWritableControlValues` refuses those on the way in.

That last guard is the same code as before but now protects the opposite
direction. It used to stop a typo from masquerading as an opt-out; it now stops
a typo from revoking one. Its docblock, the field comments on both sides of the
contract, the `od strategy` help text, and the prompt-composition note all
described the opt-in world and would have read as the reverse of the truth.

Tests carry the semantics:

- a new assertion pins the opt-out invariant, and checks not just the value
  read back but that the decision built from it actually evaluates to `off`;
- the route test now separates `default` from a saved `off`, which resolve to
  opposite routes and no longer to the same one;
- the app-config acceptance case against a real server is rewritten end to end.
  It was "nothing configured takes the ordinary route, and the same running
  daemon takes OD Next once you opt in". It is now the opt-out direction, and
  proves it from the agent invocation log rather than from the run record: the
  first run's prompt is the strategy's, the run after `off` is saved is not.

Packaged installs have no second control — the packaged child environment
allowlist carries no `OD_NEXT_*` key — so the saved mode is the only thing
standing between an opted-out user and this default.

e2e is deliberately untouched here and follows separately. Its specs mostly
never set this mode, so prototype and deck cases now take the OD Next route.
Pinning the env var in the harness is not the fix: the env var outranks the
saved config by design, which would break the spec asserting that an
app-config write takes effect with `app_config` as its source.

* test(daemon): stop the panel-grammar spec failing on the clock

`thinking-stream-panel-grammar` asserted that the whole SSE body contains
neither `Critic` nor `8.1`, on the stated premise that both "只可能来自标记内部".
That premise does not hold for the second one. The body also carries the
daemon's own `start` envelope, and `toolTokenExpiresAt` is an ISO timestamp: a
run whose token expiry lands on a second ending in `8` with milliseconds
starting with `1` produces `…:48.161Z`, which contains `8.1`. Roughly one run in
a hundred, and it hit on CI — with a thinking stream the log shows was clean,
so the spec failed on the clock rather than on a leak.

The two attribute-fragment assertions now run against the concatenated
`thinking_delta` / `text_delta` text instead of the raw body. That is not a
weaker check: persistence consumes exactly those deltas, so it is what the
spec's own "SSE clean ≡ database clean" argument was always about, and the
envelope fields it drops were never a place a leak could surface. The tag regex
stays on the whole body, where an opening `<PANELIST` cannot appear by accident.

The two prose assertions move to the same extracted text, which is what keeps
the negative assertions honest: an extractor that selected the wrong event type
would return an empty string, and every `not.toContain` would pass against it.

* feat(daemon): remove the OD Next stop latch

A run that hit certain failures wrote a row to `strategy_rollout_controls`.
From the next request on, every task on that installation took the legacy
route. The row outranked the saved mode, survived restart, and the Labs switch
kept reading "on" while the notice underneath said the harness had been paused —
with no control to unpause it. The only way back was an operator running
`od strategy rollout reset`.

The code already argued against this. The docblock over
`rolloutStopSignalForBlockedContinuation` says only a failure of the machine
contract itself may raise a latch, because an agent turn that mis-populates a
machine block "is already fail-closed for that task ... and it must not silently
return every later request in the daemon to the legacy path." One signal had
already been retired for doing exactly that: `complex_child_unverified` took OD
Next away from Codex, Claude and OpenCode because a fourth runtime lacks a
child-lifecycle producer. This generalises those narrowings instead of waiting
for the next signal to earn its own.

It also stopped being survivable. While OD Next was opt-in, the latch could only
reach the few installations that had asked for it; with the default flipped it
reaches everyone, and the population exposed to an automatic, restart-surviving,
UI-unrecoverable disable is now the whole install base.

Deleting it changes nothing about how any single failure is handled. All three
live trigger points were additive actions taken *after* the existing handling:
`native_resume_failed` already blocked the continuation, sent
`AGENT_SESSION_RESUME_FAILED` and finished the run failed; the blocked-
continuation cases were already set to `outcome: 'blocked'` with their reason
codes persisted for attribution. What goes away is only the side effect on every
later request. A fourth trigger — the run-duration threshold — never fired at
all: `OD_NEXT_STRATEGY_MAX_RUN_DURATION_MS` has no default anywhere, so the
comparison ran against NaN.

What is removed: the table and its migration, the write path and its telemetry
module, the single read in the run route, the reset endpoint, the
`od strategy rollout reset` subcommand, the latched lock in the Labs switch and
its 19 locale strings, and five contract types. `readOdNextRolloutControlStatus`
stays but no longer takes a database — the effective mode is now a pure function
of the requested mode and the content flags, so two callers reading it at the
same moment cannot disagree. Status is still worth an endpoint because
`requestedModeSource` names the authority, and `default` and a saved `off`
resolve to opposite routes.

Installations currently holding a latch recover on their own: with nothing left
to read the row, their next run is admitted normally. No migration needed, and a
downgrade is safe — older code recreates the table, reads it empty, and treats
the installation as unlatched.

Tests carry the invariant rather than a list. The cases that pinned which
signals were allowed to latch are replaced by one that pins the shape: the
decision is a function of the policy and this run's facts and takes no argument
through which an earlier run could reach it, so there is no signal left to
enumerate and none can be added by accident. The real-server case now asserts
that status still reports the deciding authority while both the reset endpoint
and its CLI subcommand are gone.

* fix(daemon): never leave the harness switch stuck, whatever the config says

Field report from a packaged build of this branch: the Design Harness switch
read on, greyed out, with "detected a problem, generation is using the original
approach" underneath, and every task on the machine taking the legacy route.
Nothing in the UI could clear it.

The diagnostics name the cause exactly. One agent turn ended mid-block —
`Unclosed <open-design-plan-contract> block`, 2 characters of visible text — and
that raised `machine_contract_leak`, whose stop mode is `off`, not `observe`. A
truncated response took the whole install off OD Next; the next daemon start
logged `requestedMode: 'active'`, `effectiveMode: 'off'`,
`od_next_rollout_stop_latched`, which is the screenshot.

That is not a rare condition. A stream ending early is the most ordinary failure
an agent has, and flipping the default hands it the entire install base.

Three changes, one property: the switch a user can see is a switch a user can
use.

1. The stop latch is removed (previously PR #7879, folded in here). A build that
   defaults on and still ships an automatic, restart-surviving, UI-unrecoverable
   disable is not shippable as two PRs — the window between them is exactly the
   build that was reported. Everything the latch did on top of the existing
   per-task handling is gone; the per-task handling is untouched.

2. An unreadable saved config no longer reads as an unconfigured one. The read
   path kept two states apart where it needed three: no file at all, a readable
   choice, and a config that exists but cannot be believed — malformed JSON, a
   non-object body, a mode this build does not recognise. The third used to
   collapse into the first harmlessly, because unconfigured meant `off` and so
   did an opt-out. Now unconfigured means `active`, so the same collapse turns
   "we cannot read your choice" into "you chose OD Next", against the
   installations most likely to have chosen the opposite. It resolves to `off`
   instead — the only answer that cannot override a real decision, and the
   recoverable one, since a user who never opted out sees the switch off and can
   turn it back on. `assertWritableControlValues` was never enough here: it
   guards writes through the API and can say nothing about a file that arrived
   bad, was hand-edited, or was written by another version.

3. A failed status read is retried from the switch instead of being permanent.
   It rendered the row locked and lifted only on remount, so a transient failure
   left a control that does nothing. A click on that lock now re-reads. The
   environment lock stays inert deliberately: the daemon would ignore the write,
   and pretending otherwise is worse than doing nothing — and no packaged
   install can reach it, since the packaged child env allowlist carries no
   `OD_NEXT_*`.

After this, the only greyed state a packaged user can reach is the moment before
the first read returns.

Installations already holding a latch recover on their own: with nothing left to
read the row, their next run is admitted normally. No migration, and a downgrade
is safe — older code recreates the table, reads it empty, and treats the
installation as unlatched.

Coverage follows the same split. The config cases run against real files through
`readAppConfig` rather than against the policy reader in isolation, because the
hole was in the join: truncated JSON, a non-object body, an unrecognised mode, a
typo, a non-string — each reads `off`, while a missing file and an explicit
`null` still reach the default. One case asserts the whole chain, saving `off`
then truncating the file and checking the mode survives, with a fresh
installation as the negative control so the guard cannot swallow the rollout it
protects. The UI case fails the first status read, clicks, and asserts the row
becomes operable.

* refactor(daemon): drop the JSDoc left above the removed latch classifier

The block described `MACHINE_CONTRACT_BOUNDARY_CODES` and
`rolloutStopSignalForBlockedContinuation`, both deleted with the stop latch.
Left in place it reads as documentation for the export below it, implying this
service still classifies machine-contract failures when it no longer does.

* fix(daemon): tell operators why `od strategy rollout reset` is gone

The command shipped in 0.21.0 and 0.21.1. Removing it left the subcommand
falling through to the generic usage dump, so an operator who scripted it saw a
list it was simply missing from and had to guess whether the command was
renamed, moved, or broken.

It now names itself: the daemon-instance stop latch it cleared no longer exists,
so there is nothing to reset, and the message points at the two commands that
replaced its use — `od config set odNextStrategyMode off` to opt out, and
`od strategy rollout status` to see which authority decides the mode.

It still exits non-zero rather than succeeding as a deprecated no-op. The
command meant "recover this machine's rollout". Reporting success for a recovery
that neither happened nor can happen is the same lie the latch itself told —
a control that says it acted while nothing changed — and this release is
removing that lie rather than relocating it into the CLI.

* fix(daemon): stop a broken config file from opting an installation out

The previous commit fixed a real hole — a saved `off` could be silently revoked
— but fixed it too widely and in the wrong direction for this rollout. It
treated a config file that failed to parse at all as evidence of an opt-out,
which it is not.

A file that will not parse resets every preference to its default: agent,
telemetry, all of it. Singling this one key out to resolve against its default
was inconsistent with the rest of the file, and the population it hits is the
wrong one — everyone whose config breaks, not everyone who opted out. Since the
second group is a subset of the first, the guard opted more installations out of
the rollout than it protected, in a change whose entire purpose is opting them
in.

The guard now covers only what it can actually see: `odNextStrategyMode` present
with a value that is not one of the modes — a hand edit, a typo, a mode written
by some other version. Something was configured and cannot be read, so it reads
`off` rather than becoming "you chose OD Next". A fresh install, a missing file,
an unparseable file and a config without the key all reach the default, which is
`active`.

That keeps both invariants this step owes: the default is on for anyone who has
not said otherwise, and a user who did say otherwise keeps their answer. The
switch stays operable in every one of these states, so nothing here can leave a
user looking at a control that does nothing.

* style(daemon): drop the blank line left at EOF by the classifier removal

The line separated `resolveAutomaticContinuationEvidence` from the JSDoc and
classifier below it. Removing those left the separator as a trailing blank line,
which `git diff --check` reports. No logic change.

* docs(daemon): stop enumerating which releases shipped `rollout reset`

The comment named 0.21.0 and 0.21.1. 0.22.0 shipped today and carries the
command too, so the enumeration was already wrong the day it was written --
any list of shipped versions goes stale by construction. Say "every release
since 0.21.0" instead, which stays true without maintenance.

The point the sentence is making is unchanged, and slightly stronger: the
surface has been out for three releases, so an operator who scripted it gets
told what happened rather than shown a help list it is missing from.

commits.commit_title: fix(web): stop a compositor scroll clamp from silently killing auto-follow (#7898)
commits.commit_message:
fix(web): stop a compositor scroll clamp from silently killing auto-follow (#7898)

* fix(web): stop a compositor scroll clamp from silently killing auto-followThe chat log decides "did the user scroll away" from one criterion: the
position got smaller AND `scrollHeight` did not change. The file's own
comment justifies that with "content-driven displacement always comes with
a `scrollHeight` change" — true for content-driven displacement, false for
a compositor clamp.Chromium keeps its own copy of how far a scroller travels so a wheel does
not have to wait on the main thread. On the chat log that copy can go stale
while layout moves on. From a real user's diagnostic bundle (Electron 41 /
Chromium 146):  scrollTop 245.5   layoutMax 718   scrollHeight 1307   unreachablePx 472.5Jump-to-latest writes `scrollTo({top: 1307})`, the position lands at 718.5
(the real layout bottom), and one wheel notch later the compositor throws it
back onto its own stale ceiling of 245.5. Content is static, so
`scrollHeight` never moves — both halves of the criterion hold, and every
clamp reads as one more user scroll-up. Auto-follow goes off without a word.The discriminator is wheel direction. A user scrolling up either carries an
upward wheel — which ChatPane's own `onWheel` already releases follow on,
ahead of the scroll event — or carries no wheel at all (scrollbar drag,
keyboard, touch). So "the only wheel in this window pointed down" is never
true of a user scroll-up; it says the user asked to move TOWARD the bottom.
A position that moves away from the bottom under that input is not their
hand. The same shape was measured independently for the freeze detector:
`scrollTop = 800`, one downward notch, thrown back to 91.The other candidates do not hold up. Landing on a known stale ceiling needs
the ceiling, which only the freeze detector's state machine can infer — and
`chat-scroll-takeover.ts` records that detector's false-positive rate as
unknown. The gap to `layoutMax` carries no information, since a user can
stop anywhere. Adjacency to a JS write is falsified by the bundle itself:
the clamp landed 3.8s after the write with zero JS write records in between,
and a window that wide swallows ordinary scrolls.This does not fix the stale ceiling — that is the takeover module's job and
it stays switched off pending a product call. It only stops the clamp from
also costing the user auto-follow.The criterion is deliberately biased to under-fire: a clamp with no wheel
witness is still treated as a user scroll-up. Welding follow on would be
worse than the bug.

* fix(web): give the wheel witness a lifetime

nettee's review on #7898 found the over-suppression this criterion was
supposed to avoid — a stale witness welding auto-follow ON, which is the
failure mode that is worse than the bug being fixed. The path is complete:

  1. the user is already at the bottom and wheels down once — the position
     does not move, so no `scroll` event fires and the witness is never
     consumed;
  2. switching conversations from the history control happens OUTSIDE the
     log element, so no pointerdown/keydown reaches it, and the effect that
     resets baseline and follow intent did not touch the witness;
  3. a later NON-wheel move to earlier content (find-in-page, a focus-driven
     scroll) is then compared against that stale downward witness, read as a
     clamp, and follow never releases.

The witness now has three independent bounds, each covering a hole the other
two cannot:

  · Consumed on use. Any scroll event spends it, including one that moves
    nothing — one witness explains one displacement, never the next.
  · Scoped to the scroll context. `WheelWitness.atScrollTop` records where
    the scroller was; the displacement's origin must be exactly that, so a
    baseline moved by anything else voids the note structurally rather than
    on a timer. Conversation switch, log node swap and panel unmount clear it
    alongside baseline and follow intent.
  · Expires after a frame. The only bound that can kill a witness no scroll
    event will ever consume. A frame is not a tuned constant: the clamp is
    dispatched in the same rendering update as the notch that caused it, and
    per the HTML update-the-rendering steps scroll events run BEFORE that
    frame's animation callbacks. (Not to be confused with the 3.8s in the
    diagnostic bundle — that is the gap between the JS write and the clamp,
    not between the wheel and the clamp.)

Recording is skipped entirely when `requestAnimationFrame` is unavailable:
without the expiry bound a witness could outlive its displacement, and no
witness just means today's behavior.

Mutation-checked line by line. Three points are honest defence in depth and
say so in-place: the conversation-switch and unmount clears cannot be turned
red today (a conversation switch always schedules a frame, and `setTab` has
no call site), and the upward-wheel counter is pinned at the predicate level
only, because `onWheel` already releases follow on an upward notch.

commits.commit_title: fix(observability): 滚动探针上报之后不该把自己关掉 (#7896)
commits.commit_message:
fix(observability): 滚动探针上报之后不该把自己关掉 (#7896)

* fix(observability): 滚动探针上报之后不该把自己关掉`Surface.reported` 同时挂着两件事:「这个 surface 的遥测已经发过了」和
「停止一切采样」。第二件是意外的 —— 这个标志被九处 listener / observer
回调读取,于是发出事件的同时也关掉了滚动采样器、滚轮通路、活动轨迹和
shortfall ledger,而 `ScrollFreezeState.reported` 在纯 detector 里做了同样
的事:`observeWheelBatch` 第一行直接 return,baseline 停在上报那一刻,
`describeSnapBackRoute` 因此永远读作 disarmed —— 偏偏那条单格路线就是为
陈旧的合成器天花板写的。真机上的代价:点击落到 718.5(布局真底部)之后 3.8 秒回到 245.5,中间零
条 JS 写入,写入拦截全程武装。而同一台机器相隔 5.4 分钟导出的三份诊断包
`stallWheelCount` 都是 83、`steps` 逐字节相同,快照写着
`blocked_by=surface_unreported` / `snapBack.armed: false`。一次标准复现
在结构上不可能被抓到。现在去重只发生在 sink:`freezeTelemetryAlreadySent()` 一个地方读这个标志,
docblock 写明规则。detector、ledger、活动环、写入拦截、snap-back 路线在
已上报的 surface 上照常运行,阈值一个没动,每个 surface 仍然只发一次
`client_chat_scroll_frozen`。内存不变:所有收集器本来就是定长环(activity / ledger.steps / ledger.probes /
transitions / write trace),总数另用计数器记,没有随时间或转录长度增长的
结构。

* fix(observability): 归因闸门要无条件跑,不能被去重挡在后面

评审说得对。上一版把遥测去重放在 inner-scroller 闸门之上,理由是省一次
祖先链遍历 —— 那是性能理由,挡不住数据正确性问题。

后果:已上报的 surface 上,用户在代码块 / 工具输出里正常滚动,那些滚轮
根本没在要求聊天记录移动,却会一路推高 stallWheelCount。因为把这一格再
拿出来的唯一动作就是那个分支里的 streak retraction,而闸门把它变成不可达。
于是一次普通的嵌套滚动,会在后续快照里长得像「聊天区连续 N 格纹丝不动」
—— 正是这把尺子要量的那个信号。尺子被自己污染,比尺子慢一点严重得多。
上一版新写的测试还把那个假的 +6 连击钉成了期望,等于在保护缺陷。

inner-scroller 闸门是归因,不是上报:这一格是打给谁的滚动条,跟事件发没
发过无关,所以它现在无条件先跑,retraction 也无条件执行。

去重仍然只有一处 —— report() 自带的 latch,每个 surface 仍然只发一次
client_chat_scroll_frozen。撤掉 report() 那行 latch 会让 16 条测试变红,
其中包括仓库里本来就有的「still refuses to report the same surface twice」。

innerScrollerSuppressions 的语义单独处理,不再靠闸门顺序保护:它的含义是
「看见了冻结却没上报」,所以计数条件收在「这个 surface 还能上报」上,
retraction 本身不受影响。规则写进字段自己的 docblock。

测试改成断言相反的事:被吸收的滚轮不把 streak 留在阈值上(每次触到就被
retract),并补一条未上报 surface 的对照,证明这个闸门的行为跟事件发没发
过无关。

已知遗留、本 PR 不动:recordCeilingProbe 在 observeWheelBatch 之前无条件
记录,被内层滚动区吸收的滚轮同样会写进 shortfall ledger。这在 main 上、
上报之前就是这样,不是这条分支引入的;要修得把归因闸门提到每一批滚轮之前
跑,那是另一个尺度的改动,单独开。

* fix(observability): 被内层滚动区吃掉的滚轮不该进 shortfall ledger

上一条只挡住了 streak,没挡住 ledger。自动评审把这半边也点出来了,是对的,
而且这半边更要紧:ledger.first 永不淘汰。

一格打给代码块的滚轮,在算术上跟真的冻结一轮完全一样 —— 聊天区确实没动,
也确实还有余量,只不过用户根本没在滚它。于是一次嵌套滚动就能永久占住
shortfall_first_*,也就是整份报告最主要被读的那个字段。streak 还能靠
retraction 拿回来,first 拿不回来,所以只能在写进去之前就拦掉。

做法:归因(countAbsorbingScrollers)提到每个带滚轮的帧的开头问一次,一个
答案同时供 ledger 和冻结判定用。原来「太贵所以只在上报时问」的理由经不起
读代码:那是从滚轮目标到聊天区的祖先链,量级是嵌套深度不是转录长度,滚轮
打在聊天区自己身上时直接返回,absorbsWheelInDirection 先用几何量筛掉再考虑
getComputedStyle,而且此处布局刚被上一句 scrollHeight 读干净。冻结路径上原
本那次调用现在被复用,不是新增。

注意这条也改变了未上报 surface 的 ledger 内容(少了被吸收滚轮那些轮次),
所以 shortfall_first_* 的取值会变 —— 变准,但确实变了。事件名、属性、类型、
每 surface 一次的基数都没动。

测试补两条断言:被吸收的滚轮在已上报 surface 上不增加 probeCount 也不改
probes;未上报的对照 surface probeCount 为 0、first 为 null。

* fix(observability): 撤回裁决不该连带抹掉「已上报」这条记录

这条是我自己引进来的,而且正好是我写 docblock 要消除的那个模式:我把
ScrollFreezeState.reported 重新定义成「永久记录:detector 已经判过一次
冻结」,然后把下面那行无条件写 false 的代码留在原地。

之前它不会出事,是因为上报之后滚轮通路整个是关的,这个分支根本到不了。
这个 PR 把通路打开了,分支就变成上报后可达:observeWheelBatch 返回
reported: true 的状态,紧接着被撤回逻辑写成 false,于是快照上出现
surface.reported: true 配 detector.reported: false —— 恰好说给同时看这
两个字段的那个人听,而且跟我刚写下的契约自相矛盾。

改成从 active.reported 取:上报前撤回仍然回到 false(裁决被丢弃,没有事件
发出,这个 surface 之后还要能上报真正的冻结),上报后保持 true(事件确实
发出去了,这就是那条记录)。撤回的是裁决,不是历史。

测试两侧都钉:已上报 surface 撤回后 detector.reported 仍为 true、
surface_unreported 仍判 false;未上报对照 surface 撤回后为 false、
surface_unreported 仍判 true。

commits.commit_title: fix(web): keep a failed question-form turn in the transcript (#7900)
commits.commit_message:
fix(web): keep a failed question-form turn in the transcript (#7900)

Answering an inline question form opens a new turn on screen before
POST /api/runs has returned a runId. When that create never yields a run,
ProjectView's stream onError deletes the optimistic assistant row by
design (no agent process ever existed) and keeps only the user row,
stamped sendFailed, with its always-on Retry. It also clears the global
error banner.

buildChatRenderItems then hid that row too: it skips every user message
starting with `[form answers`, because a delivered answer is already
summarized on the assistant message above it (#5496). That premise does
not hold for an answer that never reached a turn, so the failed round
lost its only evidence and its only way back — the round the user
watched start simply vanished, with no error, no card and no retry,
while the form stayed locked as answered.

Hide a form-answer row only when it did not fail to send, and strip the
`[form answers - <id>]` routing header from the bubble so the visible
row shows the user's own answers instead of the machine payload. Resend
still replays the untouched content.

Red spec: apps/web/tests/components/ChatPane.question-form-send-failed.test.tsx

commits.commit_title: fix(e2e): stop the packaged mac first-run gate failing on budget alone (#7899)
commits.commit_message:
fix(e2e): stop the packaged mac first-run gate failing on budget alone (#7899)

The `[P0] cold first Home run` packaged mac case has been red on almost
every beta build for eleven days (1 pass in 12 attempts) and nobody saw
it, because release-beta's smoke step is `continue-on-error: true`.

Four changes, in the order they matter:

1. Capture evidence before cleanup. A failing case uninstalled the app
   and the next case deleted the runtime namespace, so the only surviving
   trace was `logs: {skipped: true}`. The failure path now writes the
   desktop log, a raw `/api/runs` diagnostics snapshot, and the error into
   the release report before anything is torn down.

2. Give the wait a budget that matches the chain, split in two. 15s had to
   cover cold project creation through rendered output; it is now 60s for
   "the daemon owns a finished run" plus 30s for "the output surfaced", so
   a timeout says which half broke instead of leaving three observations
   that cannot falsify each other. Polling moved inside the page: every
   sample used to cost a `tools-pack mac inspect` process, which ate about
   a third of the old budget on its own.

3. Drop the injected 503. `POST /api/runs` does not answer
   WORKSPACE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE — local run creation is deliberately
   independent of Workspace membership availability — so the case spent
   an extra create round trip plus a 500ms backoff on a branch production
   cannot reach. Run-create retry semantics stay covered by
   apps/web/tests/providers/sse.test.ts.

4. Make the exempted red audible. The exemption stays (at a 1/12 pass rate
   a blocking gate would stall the daily beta), but `tools-release
   write-report` now turns a failed smoke into a run annotation and a
   caution banner at the top of the step summary.

commits.commit_title: feat(ci): publish the What's New card from the repository (#7892)
commits.commit_message:
feat(ci): publish the What's New card from the repository (#7892)

* feat(ci): publish the What's New card from the repository

Move the post-update highlight document into the repo and publish it from
GitHub Actions, so changing the card is a pull request instead of a task
that needs personal Cloudflare credentials.

- docs/whats-new.json is the source of truth, next to its spec doc.
- pnpm guard validates it through the daemon's own parser on every PR, so a
  document that would silently show no card cannot merge.
- whats-new-publish.yml uploads on merge to main (and on manual dispatch,
  with a read-only dry-run mode) and verifies the object by reading it back
  from the origin the daemon fetches, past the edge cache.

* docs: name the CI job that actually runs the guard check

* fix(ci): gate the What's New publish behind a main-only environment

A workflow_dispatch runs the workflow file from the ref it is dispatched
against, so the in-workflow main-only assertion was editable by whoever
triggered it: anyone with write access could publish unreviewed content to
every installed client from their own branch.

Split the workflow so credentials live in one place and that place is gated by
GitHub rather than by YAML. `validate` holds no secrets and runs on any ref;
`publish` declares the `whats-new-publish` environment, whose deployment-branch
policy allows main only and which owns the R2 secrets. Dropping the environment
declaration to escape the branch policy also drops the secrets.

Also points the card at the new Arena URLs supplied by product.

* fix(ci): pin the What's New publish trust boundary in a check that runs

The missing-credentials error still told operators the R2 keys are
repository secrets. Following that string is the exact setup the previous
revision closed: repository secrets are readable from any job on any
branch, so a modified workflow dispatched from an unreviewed ref could
publish to every installed client — or just take the keys. Point the
error at the `whats-new-publish` environment and refuse the repository
path in the same breath.

The boundary itself had no coverage: nothing read the workflow, so moving
`environment:` or a `secrets.*` expression back onto the arbitrary-ref
job would stay green while still publishing correctly from main.

That coverage cannot be lane-routed. Running the planner over
`.github/workflows/whats-new-publish.yml` selects neither
`web_tests_required` nor `ui_p0_validation_required`, so the `e2e_vitest`
workload does not run for a workflow-only edit — an assertion living only
there would be skipped for exactly the change class it guards. The check
therefore lives in `pnpm guard`, which CI invokes from the unconditional
preflight job, same reasoning as the document guard next to it.

It asserts that the credential-bearing job declares the environment by
its exact name, needs `validate` and is gated on its output with no
`always()`/`cancelled()` escape, reads all four bucket bindings, and that
no other job attaches an environment or reads any secret at all.

The e2e suite drives it over the real workflow mutated into each of those
regressions in turn, so every assertion is proven able to fail; gutting
the checker turns all eleven red.

* chore(whats-new): seed the document from the live card

Bringing the workflow in with new copy attached ties the infrastructure to
a content decision. The Arena CTA this document pointed at is not live —
`/llm-arena-for-design/` and `/zh/llm-arena/llm-arena-for-design/` both
404 — and the card renders regardless, so merging would have put a dead
button on every client's Home.

Seed the repository copy from the object that is already serving instead:
byte-identical to `https://whatsnew.open-design.ai/whats-new.json`, id
`0.21.0`. That puts the current state under version control and makes the
first automatic publish idempotent — it uploads exactly what is already
there, so the merge exercises the whole chain (validate, upload, read-back
against the origin the daemon fetches) without changing anything a user
sees.

The Arena copy is not lost; it moves to the PR body as a follow-up for the
release owner, who can now change the card through this workflow without
holding personal Cloudflare credentials.

* fix(ci): detect secrets by context, not by access shape

The guard added last round matched `${{ secrets.NAME }}` with a regex over
the raw workflow text. A guard whose whole job is to stop a secret reaching
the arbitrary-ref job had a blind spot for most of the ways to read one.

Verified against the previous implementation, each returning zero
violations while a secret reached `validate`: `secrets['NAME']`,
`secrets["NAME"]`, `secrets [ 'NAME' ]`, `secrets . NAME`,
`toJSON(secrets)`, a bare `secrets`, and `fromJSON(toJSON(secrets)).NAME`.

Extending the regex would have repeated the mistake that caused it. One
bypass proves why: a double-quoted YAML scalar may carry a backslash line
continuation, so

    STOLEN: "${{ sec\
      rets.NAME }}"

parses to a live secret read while the source text contains no such
substring. No text scanner can see that, however many shapes it lists.

So the workflow is read through a YAML parser, and detection is a single
property instead of an enumeration: GitHub's expression language has no
string-to-context evaluation, so a secret cannot be reached without naming
the `secrets` context as an identifier. Finding that identifier inside any
`${{ … }}` expression covers every access form, including ones nobody has
thought of.

Parsing also retires the hand-rolled job splitter and its own failure
modes, and lets the check distinguish "no violations" from "nothing was
examined" — an unparseable document, a flow-style jobs mapping, or a
renamed publish job now fail closed rather than passing quietly.

Two holes the shape list never covered are closed as a side effect: a
job-level `secrets:` key passes credentials to a called workflow with no
expression at all, and workflow-level `env:` is inherited by every job.

`yaml@2.9.0` becomes a root devDependency. It was already in the lockfile
via `tools/release` and pinned repository-wide by the existing pnpm
override, so the lockfile gains only the root importer entry.

Test coverage moves with it: 26 of 46 cases now go red when the checker is
gutted, up from 11.

---------

Co-authored-by: lefarcen <ontf116@gmail.com>

commits.commit_title: fix(web): give an invalid API key its own error card (#7893)
commits.commit_message:
fix(web): give an invalid API key its own error card (#7893)

* fix(web): give an invalid API key its own error card

A BYOK run that fails because the user's API key is wrong renders the
generic fallback card: 「任务执行失败」 + 「这次没能顺利完成……把日志发给我们」
+ 〔联系支持〕. The daemon had already classified it exactly right
(category `auth`, detail `invalid_api_key`, user_action `login`), but
`invalid_api_key` appeared zero times in `apps/web/src`, so the run fell
through every mapping table to the last-resort card. The result is that
a wrong API key sends the user to customer support, with no entry point
to the screen that holds the key.

Add the S05 row (`DETAIL_FAILURE_UI`), copy verbatim from the product
error-copy doc, and reuse the existing 〔去设置〕 action
(`onOpenSettings('execution')`) — the same destination the send-time
BYOK preflight gate already uses.

* fix(web): scope the invalid-key Settings action to BYOK agents

`invalid_api_key` is read off the flattened stderr of EVERY agent
(`authDetail`, apps/daemon/src/run-failure-classification.ts), so the new
S05 row was also claiming local CLI runs. A `claude` that prints
`Invalid API key · Please run /login` arrives as
`AGENT_AUTH_REQUIRED` + `invalid_api_key`, and the row — which resolves
before the code branches — replaced its S02 「{agent} 尚未登录」 +
terminal-login guidance with a button that opens a screen where that key
cannot be changed. `opencode` / `kimi` / `qwen` have no key field in the
`execution` section at all.

Scope the card to the tier whose key we actually hold: the BYOK / API
provider agents. `byokApiKeyIsEditableInSettings`
(apps/web/src/utils/byokProvider.ts) is the same line the send-time BYOK
gate draws — `ProjectView.requiresByokPreflight` is
`mode === 'api' || agentId === 'byok-opencode'`, and a `mode === 'api'`
run is stamped onto its message as one of the eight `*-api` ids from
`API_PROTOCOL_AGENT_IDS`. That table moves to `byokProvider.ts` (which
has runtime-free imports) so `runtime/amr-guidance.ts` can read it
without pulling the provider stack in; `utils/apiProtocol.ts` imports it
back.

Everything outside that tier keeps the path it had before this branch:
`AGENT_AUTH_REQUIRED` / `UNAUTHORIZED` fall through to the existing S02
card, Antigravity keeps its terminal-auth branch (it resolves earlier),
AMR keeps S04. No new copy and no new i18n key — S02 is already in use.

Red check: removing the `byokApiKeyIsEditableInSettings` guard turns the
two native-CLI cases red with the bug itself —
`expected 'chat.runError.title.apiKeyInvalid Claude' to contain
'chat.runError.title.signInRequired.other'`.

commits.commit_message:
fix(daemon): keep the failure verdict alive from the watchdog to the card (#7884)

* fix(daemon): name the ACP stage-timeout verdict instead of writing prose

The ACP stage watchdog is the daemon's own verdict — nothing upstream
reports anything, the daemon decides a stage is over and kills the child.
It shipped that verdict as a bare `{ message: 'ACP <stage> timed out after
<n>ms' }`, so the only thing that could recover "this run timed out"
downstream was a regex over that English sentence (`isTimeoutText`). Any
path that rewrites, wraps, localizes or drops an ACP error message re-filed
a watchdog kill as `process_exit / exit_code` — `retryable: false`,
`user_action: 'none'` — which is the generic card with no Retry, for a
failure whose entire remedy is a retry.

The watchdog now stamps `retryable: true` and `details.kind = 'timeout'`
(the same discriminator `acp_child_exit` / `acp_no_visible_output` /
`amr_model` already carry), and the classifier reads that marker rather
than re-deriving the verdict from the sentence. The sentence itself is
unchanged: it is what the details drawer shows and what telemetry reads.

Deliberately narrow — only the watchdog writes the marker, and only the
timeout branch reads it. Agent-supplied JSON-RPC data lands under
`error.data`, never `error.details`, so an agent cannot forge the verdict;
`empty_output` still resolves first, so a run that stalled AND produced
nothing still says it produced nothing.

`acp-stall-last-progress-age` re-anchors its non-vacuity guard on the
child's own exit status (143 = its SIGTERM handler ran) instead of on the
derived `AGENT_EXIT_143` code, which never described this failure.

* fix(daemon): recognise opencode's compaction-continuation stream EOF

vela 0.0.35 (#1847) moved the compaction continuation onto its own request
and worded its EOF differently: `opencode compaction continuation ended
before prompt completion`. That phrase matched nothing in the repository,
so the same bridge-level stream EOF the resume-failure table already
handles — one phase later — could not reach the re-seed path at all and
ended the conversation on a hard failure.

Added to `AMR_OPENCODE_EVENT_STREAM_RESUME_FAILURE_PATTERNS` in the same
shape as its siblings (un-anchored, case-insensitive), so a compaction that
dies mid-continuation clears the stale handle and re-runs the turn with a
fresh session — one slightly slower cold turn instead of a dead end.

The gate stays narrow: `resolveAgentResumeFailurePolicy` only fires when a
stored handle was actually being continued (`isResuming` + a resume session
id), and `run.resumeAutoReseeded` allows the recovery once. A create turn
carrying the same phrase is untouched.

* fix(daemon): keep an upstream that says "retryable" retryable

Real corpus (2026-09-08, runs 423140d1 and e9bea966): opencode reported a
closed upstream socket AFTER exhausting its own three attempts and said so
in machine-readable form — `"isRetryable": true`. The daemon recorded
`upstream_unavailable / stream_disconnected` with `retryable: false`, the
opposite of what upstream stated.

Where the word was dropped: opencode's field is `isRetryable`, and vela
hands the whole `session.error` envelope over as a JSON string inside the
ACP error message rather than as `error.data`. `rpcErrorRetryable` read
only `data.retryable`; the classifier's `latestRetryable` reads
`error.data.isRetryable` and never saw it either. With no verdict from
either reader, `fail()` fell back to its own `retryable: false` default,
and that fabricated verdict became the run's.

The cost is not the error card (`stream_disconnected` still draws a Retry)
but the daemon's own recovery: `isResumableFailure` returns false the
moment `retryable` is false, so `run.resumable` never gets set and the
Continue affordance disappears, and `decidePostToolResumeRecovery` requires
`retryable === true`, so the silent post-tool continuation never fires.

Both readers now accept the `isRetryable` spelling. Only `true` is read: an
explicit upstream "no" is already handled by the branches that can disprove
it (a 4xx re-fails identically and routes to `upstream_client_error`), and
letting a coarse SDK flag force `false` is drift the classifier refuses by
name. `request_too_large` still wins over it.

Verified against the frozen ACP landing table: no row moves. Removing
`fail()`'s `?? false` default instead would have moved 17 of them,
including turning a 429 rate limit into a retry — left alone deliberately.

* fix(daemon): read a structural isRetryable only when it says true

`rpcErrorRetryable` accepted the vendor `isRetryable` field in both
directions, so an adapter that forwards opencode's `error.data` object
structurally (rather than embedded in the message string, which is the
shape the corpus happened to carry) could hand the bridge a `false`.

`session.ts` composes the two readers with `??`, so that `false` did not
merely record an upstream "no": it short-circuited
`inferRpcErrorRetryable`, which for the same payload in string form
returns `undefined` and lets a transport blip be read as retryable.
`fail()` then stamped `retryable: false`, the classifier adopted it as
`retryableHint`, and `isResumableFailure` withdrew Continue — the exact
failure this branch exists to remove, reachable through the other shape.

Read only `true`, matching the rule `inferRpcErrorRetryable` already
applies to the string form. ACP's own `retryable` keeps both values: it
is a deliberate protocol-level statement, not a status-code-derived SDK
flag riding along inside a vendor payload.

Red spec covers the structural shape the previous negative test did not:
parity between the two shapes on the real 404 `error.data`, and a
structural `isRetryable:false` on the row-B1 stream-idle-timeout blip
that must not overrule the classifier. Both go red with this change
backed out. The frozen ACP landing table is untouched — 47 rows, 17
moved-code rows, 196 assertions, zero lines changed.

* fix(daemon): namespace the ACP watchdog verdict so agent data cannot claim it

`error.details` is not a daemon-private slot. `fail()` copies an agent's
JSON-RPC `error.data` into it verbatim (`fail(rpcErr, { details })`), so an
adapter sending `{"error":{"data":{"kind":"timeout"}}}` reached
`hasDaemonTimeoutVerdict` as a stage-watchdog kill: `failure_category:
'timeout'`, `terminal_trigger: 'acp_stage_timeout'`, and precedence over
the forced-signal guard — with the watchdog never having fired.

Rename the marker to `acp_stage_timeout` and match that exact value, so no
upstream payload collides with it by accident. Both docblocks now describe
the shared slot accurately, including the residual: this is collision
resistance, not authentication. An adapter that deliberately sent
`kind: 'acp_stage_timeout'` would still be believed, and closing that needs
a daemon-only field agent payload is never copied into — noted at `fail()`,
not done here.

The previous anti-forgery test asserted this against `error.data`, a shape
the session bridge never emits, so it passed without exercising the copy.
Replaced with one that drives the real bridge: the agent answers
`session/prompt` with a JSON-RPC error carrying `error.data`, and the frame
the bridge actually emits is what gets classified. It also pins the copy
itself, so a future change that stops forwarding agent data is visible.
Added the matching positive control through the same real bridge.

Backing both source lines out turns 4 tests red, in both directions.
Frozen ACP landing table untouched: 47 rows, 17-entry moved list, 196/196,
zero lines changed.

commits.commit_title: fix(web): restore the product's run-error copy across 19 locales (#7887)
commits.commit_message:
fix(web): restore the product's run-error copy across 19 locales (#7887)

* fix(web): use the product doc's polished copy on run error cards

Six run-error cards were showing copy engineering had written, not the
copy product signed off. The authoritative source is the Feishu doc
"运行报错场景文案", whose每格 carries three things: 原文时机, a draft
「原文提示」 (with buttons and slots), and the table's 润色标题 / 润色正文.
Only the last two are final — S30's card had been transcribed from the
draft column.

Replaced verbatim, across all 19 locales:

  S07  AMR_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE      当前模型不可用
  S12  timeout / inactivity       等待回复超时
  S13  model_not_supported …      当前模型不支持此任务   (new card)
  S22  AGENT_RUNTIME_DEF_INVALID  Open Design 运行异常
  S23  ARTIFACT_NOT_FOUND         暂无可预览的文件       (body was null)
  S30  the five environment causes 当前地区暂不支持此服务

Two structural fixes the copy forced:

- S13 is two rows in the doc ("模型不存在" and "模型能力不支持"), and S07
  is a third. One title key served all three. Split out
  `title.modelCapabilityUnsupported` + its message so the three sentences
  stop overwriting each other.
- S23's message key was null, so the card fell through to the generic
  「这次没能顺利完成」 — a run that ENDED NORMALLY was being described as a
  failure, with nothing said about what to do. The doc has a sentence for
  it; it is now wired.

Not changed, and why:

- S08 供应商额度用完 and S13 模型不存在 need {供应商} / {模型名}; S16 needs
  {套餐名}; S07 并发上限 needs {N}. None of those values reach the error
  card — the failure event carries only code / failureDetail / the raw
  upstream string. Rather than putting a literal `{模型名}` in front of a
  user, those cells wait for a data path.
- `title.quotaExhausted` still serves both S08 and S15; splitting it is
  moot while both consumers are blocked (S08 on {供应商}, S15 on a routing
  ruling).

Red spec: apps/web/tests/components/ChatPane.run-error-copy-from-spec.test.tsx
asserts the rendered card text (title line + chat-run-error-description),
not keys or classes. 27 assertions red before this change, green after,
and red again when the implementation is reverted.

* fix(web): stop diagnosing local failures as a regional block

S30's polished copy («当前地区暂不支持此服务» / «暂不支持当前网络所在地区，
请尝试切换网络后再试。») was wired to all five client-environment details.
None of them is a regional block, so the card told users their region was
unsupported and to switch networks after a local SQLite/WAL write failed.

Evidence — `clientEnvironmentFailureDetail`
(`apps/daemon/src/run-failure-classification.ts:299-306`) is the only producer
of these five, and each matches something local:

  host_policy_block      Windows Application Control / AppLocker
  local_storage_failure  SQLite/WAL I/O, readonly, locked, corrupt
  certificate_failure    certificate / CERT_ / self-signed / unable to verify
  proxy_configuration    unsupported proxy protocol / proxy configuration
  network_configuration  ENOTFOUND / ECONNREFUSED / EHOSTUNREACH / getaddrinfo

The clincher: the daemon does detect a regional block, and it is not one of
these. `Country, region, or territory not supported` matches
`isUpstreamClientErrorText` and lands on `upstream_client_error` — a detail this
card never reaches (pinned by `run-failure-classification.test.ts:1375`).

The product doc's S30 table has exactly one polished row, and its 「场景内的情况」
is 「地区不支持」. No polished cell exists for certificate, proxy, host policy or
local storage, so there is nothing to copy verbatim for those. Rather than
invent wording, all five keep their previous copy and carry 待拍板 notes naming
the missing cell.

Also removes the five S30 rows from the verbatim-copy matrix (they were never
doc cells) and adds the invariant: no client-environment detail may render a
regional diagnosis, and each still names its own cause.

Refs PR #7887 review thread PRRT_kwDOSOgY8s6gJ452.

commits.commit_title: fix(chat): make the failure card, the queued action and the fork note stop disappearing (#7871)
commits.commit_message: fix(chat): make the failure card, the queued action and the fork note stop disappearing (#7871) * fix(web): ellipsize the fork divider note instead of hard-cutting it The fork divider footnote lost its ellipsis when #7863 merged the two-block layout into one line. `.fork-note` became `display: flex` so the branch icon and the label could sit side by side, but the three truncation declarations (`overflow: hidden`, `text-overflow: ellipsis`, `white-space: nowrap`) stayed on `.fork-sep span` — the very same element. Bare text inside a flex container lives in an anonymous flex item, and `text-overflow` is not inherited, so the anonymous box falls back to `clip`: the 62% cap still clipped, just without the three dots. Move the label into its own `.fork-note-label` span and hang the truncation on that layer, with `min-width: 0` to release the flex item's default `min-width: auto`. `.fork-sep span` becomes `.fork-sep > span` so the inner label is not pinned to `flex: none` — a non-shrinkable flex item is always exactly as wide as its content and can never overflow. Also finishes OPEND-2714's copy: the 16 locales other than en / zh-CN / zh-TW still carried translations of the retired English sentence. They now say what `Continued from chat` says, each within 1.5x the English length so they stay inside the 62% cap. * test(web): witness the fork note ellipsis in a browser, not in chat.css apps/web/src/components/chat/AGENTS.md §5 forbids asserting CSS class names or declarations in chat tests, and the spec added in the previous commit did exactly that: it located the label by className, parsed chat.css, and pinned the resolved values of text-overflow, overflow, white-space, min-width and flex. Delete it. Replace it with a narrow browser witness. e2e/ui/fork-note-ellipsis.test.ts forks a conversation through the real daemon endpoint, renders it in the longest shipped locale (German), squeezes the chat panel until the label overflows, then checks two observable things: the label really is overflowing its box, and its paint differs from the same element forced to `text-overflow: clip`. Comparing the element against itself keeps the oracle baseline-free, and a build that still hard-cuts paints identically under both, so the check cannot pass vacuously. Asserting the declarations was the wrong instrument anyway: the broken build declared `text-overflow: ellipsis` too. What was wrong was the box it sat on, and only a laid-out browser can see that. The one structural fact worth keeping - the label is carried by its own element rather than as bare text beside the icon - moves into the existing fork-divider spec and keys off a data-testid instead of a class name. Enrolls the new file in the project-workspace UI P0 group. An unenrolled P1 would run only in the prerelease full pool, which means shipping a witness that nothing on the merge path ever executes. * test(e2e): wait for the fork divider before squeezing the chat panel The width squeeze is a raw custom-property write onto the split, which React's own width effect would overwrite if a late fetch re-rendered between the write and the measurement. Wait for the divider to paint at the default width first, then squeeze with nothing awaited in between. Also corrects a stale doc comment that named a helper this file never had. * fix(e2e): squeeze the chat panel without racing its width transition CI caught the guard doing exactly what it was written to catch: it failed with "content 161px vs box 161px", meaning the note never overflowed and the ellipsis check would have been measuring nothing. The cause was the squeeze, not the copy. `--project-chat-panel-width` is a registered `@property` with a 200ms transition, so writing it tweens from the default 460px and the measurement taken right after read the panel mid-flight. Suspend the transition the way the product's own resize handle does (`.is-resizing-chat`), and do the write and the read inside a single evaluate so no re-render can land between them. Also measures the label before and after the squeeze, so the next failure names its own cause: a panel that never narrowed is a fixture problem, a narrowed panel that still fits the text is a copy problem. The previous message could not tell those apart. * chore(web): drop the now-unused splitList export from the cascade helper It was exported only to feed the CSS-parsing spec that the previous commit deleted. Nothing outside the helper calls it any more, so put it back to a module-private function and leave the shared test infrastructure exactly as it was on main. * fix(web): collapse the queued row's leading action into one 「引导对话」 button The queued-send row's leading action had two faces: a 74px labelled 「引导对话」 while `canSteerCurrentTurn` held, and an unlabelled 22px "send now" icon otherwise. Both were wired to the same `sendQueuedChatSendNow` — the gate only changed the name, the tooltip and the analytics `element` value. Product ruled on 2026-09-08: 「引导对话就是原本的立即发送啊,只不过我们 换了个名字跟 codex 客户端对齐了下」. So the gate goes, the fallback face goes, and the row keeps one button that is always 「引导对话」. The delivered spec agrees. `729fa43ce7:docs/design/chat-panel-next.html` component 17 "Queue" draws exactly one action there — `aria-label="引导对话" data-tip="引导对话"` with `引导对话` — and never the icon-only send-now key. `data-tip` is the plain name, so `title` / `data-tooltip` / `aria-label` collapse from `chat.queuedSteerInterrupts` back to `chat.queuedSteer`; visible text and accessible name are now identical (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name). Order is untouched: steer → edit → delete (OPEND-2715). Analytics: this surface no longer emits `ui_click` with `element: 'send_now'`. The surviving button reports `'steer'`, matching the name it now carries. The `send_now` member stays in the contract union because PostHog still holds the historical events. Props: `onSteerQueuedSend` existed only to carry the gate, so it is removed from ChatPane, SideChatTab and both ProjectView call sites, along with `canSteerCurrentTurn`. `onSendQueuedNow` survives as the single handler — it has the second pass-through face in `SideChatTab`'s `controlledChat`, and it names what the handler actually does. `steerBlockedReason` is left alone: it had no producer before this change either, and retiring a deliberately parked placeholder is its own call. * fix(prompts): stop asking the model for a per-question help string OPEND-2707. The clarification card stopped rendering the per-question subtitle (`q.help`) in #7863, but the prompt layer kept asking the model to write one — so the model spent tokens on copy nobody would ever see, and believed it had already told the user something it had not. The user ruled on 2026-09-08 to go all the way and retire the prompt half too. Three prompt surfaces carried it: - `core-slim.ts` routed leftover context into "the individual question labels/help"; context now has one destination, the question label. - The UI locale override (daemon + contracts mirror) listed "helper text" among the question-form controls that must be localized — naming the field without naming it. The other four entries in that list all still render. - The ElevenLabs voice picker is the only form the repo itself authors, and it shipped the only `help` string in the tree. Its content is real information (the visible labels are voice descriptions; the submitted value is the voice_id), so it moves into the question label rather than being dropped. `FormQuestion` has no per-question `description`, and `placeholder` is already taken by "Choose a voice". That form is `JSON.stringify`d whole into the system prompt, so it doubles as the model's worked example of what a question may look like — leaving a `help` key there would have quietly undone the rest of the change. `e2e/tests/question-form-help-retired.test.ts` guards all seven authorized prompt paths, mirroring `question-form-visual-style-retired.test.ts`. It reads source bytes, so it also asserts the parser keeps tolerating `help` — the dormant field must not be removed along with the prompt guidance. Snapshot: only `totalChars` moves, on the three scenarios that compose the touched text; no section is added or removed. * docs(web): record FormQuestion.help as dormant, not dead OPEND-2707 follow-up. With the renderer, the CSS rule, the prompt guidance and the last host-authored producer all gone, `help` now has no producer and no consumer anywhere in the tree. It still stays. Removing `help?: string` would break `QuestionForm.no-question-subtitle.test.tsx` and `QuestionForm.test.tsx` — and the first of those is the only positive evidence that the subtitle is not rendered. Deleting a zero-cost field at the price of the test that guards the invariant is a bad trade. Cached prompts, older clients and the model's own memory of the old format can also still send a question carrying the key, and the parser should keep tolerating it rather than change parse shape as a side effect of this retirement. Same reasoning as the six `qf.visual*` i18n keys in `specs/current/chat-panel-decisions-sheet.md`. The field now documents when and why it went dormant, and how to bring the rendering half back (the pre-#7863 revision of both files). Also corrects `DesignDirection.mood` in both prompt mirrors: its docblock said the text is "shown to the user as `help`", which was already inaccurate — it is the `mood` blurb on a `direction-cards` option, and that renderer has had no call site since the visual-style question was retired. * fix(web): keep the disconnect failure card when no reconnect row is there A turn that failed with `DAEMON_STREAM_DISCONNECTED` left nothing at all on screen once the user stepped out of the project and came back: no failure card, no reconnect line, no way to retry. `anotherSurfaceOwnsFailure` in `ChatPane` handed the story to the reconnect line unconditionally, on the premise (stated in the comment right above it) that the reconnect line "is always there". It is not: `ProjectView` has a dedicated unmount effect that clears `reconnectView` on project change / screen exit, so on re-entry the card yields to a surface that has already left. The neighbouring balance rung already encodes the right invariant — `balanceCardCannotTakeTheHandoff` refuses the handoff when the upgrade card cannot be drawn. The same invariant was only written on one of the two rungs. Both rungs now name their handoff target first, then ask one shared question: is that surface actually present. Red spec: `ChatPane.error-card-ladder.test.tsx` — a disconnected run with no reconnect row must render the card, its own `chat.connectionDropped` copy, and a retry action. Reverse anchor (row present -> no card) is green on both sides of the fix. The two older cases in that file asserted "no card" while rendering *without* a reconnect row: they pinned this defect rather than the invariant. Both now put the handoff target on screen, so they pin what they were written for — that either signal (structured code, or a legacy detail-only row) is recognized as the disconnect failure. * fix(web): shorten the Cloud switch CTA to match the delivery spec The error card's primary button read 「切换到 OpenDesign Cloud 并重试」 while the delivery spec (docs/design/chat-panel-next.html, cell 79 "特殊错误 · 运行环境为 CLI / BYOK") writes 「切换到 Cloud」. Product ruled in person on 2026-09-08: "切换到 cloud 就行了,你怎么写那么 长的文案『切换到 Cloud 并重试』" and "具体的报错文案不一定跟设计稿对齐, 按钮文案对齐先". So only `chat.amrCard.switchCta` is aligned here — the card's title and body keep their own product copy and are deliberately left untouched, including the separate `chat.amrCard.switchBody` key. All 19 locales are shortened to the same "Switch to Cloud" register with the trailing "and retry" clause dropped. Comments in ChatPane.tsx and amr-guidance.ts that quoted the old label are updated so they stop describing copy that no longer exists; the reasoning around them is unchanged. Playwright assertions in e2e/ui that pinned the old label follow the new string. * docs(specs): record the three rulings taken on 2026-09-08 * fix(web): keep the failure card when a failed turn has no words for it A turn that ends in a terminal failure loses its entire recovery surface whenever the card cannot compute a description. The whole card — title, message, and all four actions (contact support, export logs, retry, switch to Cloud) — hangs off one `displayError` ternary, so a null description takes the explanation and every way out with it. What is left on screen is the execution shell's bare "run failed" line, written on the assumption that the card below it says why. The three description sources all go empty together more often than the shape suggests: the mapping table's own last-resort row carries no `messageKey`, the pane-level `error` state is reset when ProjectView unmounts on navigation, and the run's raw detail never reached the message for the `AGENT_UNAVAILABLE` / `BYOK_PROVIDER_REQUIRED` / `AGENT_RUNTIME_DEF_INVALID` family (daemon `fail()` emits without going through `persistRunEventToAssistantMessage`) or for the `runStatus:'failed'` rows ProjectView writes itself when self-healing a phantom running turn. `resolveRunErrorCardDescription` now takes `turnEndedInTerminalFailure` and falls back to `RUN_FAILURE_FALLBACK_MESSAGE_KEY` instead of rendering nothing. It is the last branch, so every handoff and every more precise source still wins ahead of it. The signal is `retryableAssistantMessage`, which already gates the recovery entries and already treats a delivery failure (`no_result` / `delivery_failed`) as terminal, minus the empty API response — that one has a surface of its own ("No output") and must not get a second one. Also stops an empty pane-error string from shadowing the run's own detail. That branch carried a comment saying the silence was a separate question; this is the same question, answered the same way.

commits.commit_title: test(e2e): harden onboarding status mock against reload race (#7699)
commits.commit_message:
test(e2e): harden onboarding status mock against reload race (#7699)

* test(e2e): harden onboarding status mock against reload race

wireOnboardingMocks wrote window.__amrOnboardingStatusCalls via
page.evaluate inside the vela/status route handler. When the
reload tests intentionally reloaded the page, an in-flight status
poll could evaluate against a destroyed execution context and fail
the test before its reload assertions ran.

Wrap the instrumentation writes in a narrow safeEvaluate helper
that only swallows navigation-destroyed errors and re-throws all
other failures, preserving strict reload/cancel assertions.

commits.commit_title: feat(release): alert through the other Feishu bot when the prerelease card goes silent (#7873)
commits.commit_message:
feat(release): alert through the other Feishu bot when the prerelease card goes silent (#7873)

* feat(release): alert through the other Feishu bot when the prerelease card goes silent

The progressive card is now the only prerelease notification, and every way it
breaks is silent: the pipeline stays green, the packages ship, and the channel
hears nothing. The watcher catches Feishu failures on purpose — one hiccup must
not end a two-hour watch — so expired application-bot credentials look exactly
like a healthy run.

Adds a last-resort notice delivered through the custom-bot webhook, which is a
different bot with a different secret, so a credential failure on the card side
cannot take the alert down with it. It fires only when the card did not reach
the group: the watcher now reports `card_delivered` for a card whose FINAL state
is in the chat, and the gate reads that rather than the job result.

Two callers, mutually exclusive so a release can never draw both:
release-prerelease-card.yml's `fallback_notice` job covers a watcher that died
or never delivered; steps at the end of release-prerelease.yml's
`dispatch_validation` cover a card that was never dispatched. The latter are
steps, not a job, because nothing may appear in a `needs:` on the dispatchers.

* fix(release): keep the fallback notice reachable past the dispatch it reports

The two steps that actually deliver the notice carried no status function, so
GitHub's implicit success() skipped them whenever anything earlier in the job
had failed. `dispatch-validation.sh` exits non-zero when it cannot dispatch the
card on any ref — which marks the job failed — so on the one path the
dispatch-side fallback exists for, it was silent. This PR was written to close
the implicit-success() trap at the job level and walked into its step-level twin.

Both consumers now carry `always() && steps.notice.outcome == 'success'`: the
status function so a failed dispatch still reaches them, and the outcome check
so neither a crashed nor a skipped composer can hand feishu-notice.ts an empty
body. The composer writes `alert` last, after every field a poster reads, so
`alert=true` in an append-only $GITHUB_OUTPUT means the whole notice is on disk.

Adds the step-level reachability rule as a spec beside the existing job-level
one, and puts the dispatched prerelease lanes into that job-level sweep —
release-prerelease-card.yml was outside it, so `fallback_notice`, whose `if`
hand-checks `needs.card.result`, was uncovered by the rule it has to obey.

commits.commit_title: chore(release): stop blocking stable releases on missing release notes (#7886)
commits.commit_message:
chore(release): stop blocking stable releases on missing release notes (#7886)

A stable release with no docs/CHANGELOG/v<version>/ directory hard-failed at
the very first job. Fixing it mid-release is not "write two markdown files":
the stable promotion gate pins github.commit to the promoted prerelease, so the
changelog commit invalidates that artifact and forces a fresh ~27-minute
prerelease round trip.

Missing notes are now a loud warning instead of a failure. reviewReleaseNotePlanPolicy
returns warnings for a stable release with no notes, or one missing zh-CN, and
prepare-release-note surfaces them as a ::warning:: annotation plus a job
summary entry. Notes that exist but cannot be consumed still throw: a channel
mismatch, or a plan that omits the default locale every consumer falls back to.

publish-metadata carried a second stable gate on the same condition. Removing
only the first would have moved the hard failure past the GitHub draft release
and asset upload, which is strictly worse, so both are gone. The rest of the
chain already treated "absent" as a complete outcome — it is the beta and
prerelease path — so publication, verification, and metadata assembly are
unchanged.

Non-stable channels behave exactly as before.

commits.commit_title: test(desktop): compare PPTX captures portably instead of per-platform (#7845)
commits.commit_message:
test(desktop): compare PPTX captures portably instead of per-platform (#7845)

`comparePng` in the layered-background suite reduced every BGRA comparison
to a mean and one strict global maximum. The maximum is the whole gate for
six of the assertions, and it is not portable: on Debian the same commit,
lockfile and Electron produce 255/245/211/205/201/18 against bounds of
224/160/160/160/160/16, while Ubuntu 24.04 — the runner ci.yml uses for
`workspace_unit` — stays under every one of them. A contributor on any
other Linux sees six red tests on a clean checkout with no way to tell
them from a real regression.

The divergence is not antialiasing noise: hundreds of fully opaque pixels
carry the content in the reference capture and plain white in the isolated
export, or the reverse. Isolating an element re-renders it, so a clip,
mask, filter or text-clip boundary lands on a neighbouring pixel, and the
capture rectangle's own rounding lands on the outer frame — on one probe
608 of the 876 divergent pixels were exactly the bottom row of a 608-wide
image.

Extract the comparison into `compareBgraBitmaps` in deck-capture.ts, next
to the other pure capture helpers, and mirror it into the probe source the
way `captureUntilPainted` and `bgraBitmapHasPaint` already are. The mean
stays a strict whole-bitmap mean, so a broad fidelity loss still has
nowhere to hide. The maximum matches each pixel against the best candidate
in the 3x3 neighbourhood of the exported bitmap and skips the one-pixel
frame, which is what makes it measure fidelity rather than the host
graphics stack.

No bound is raised. Measured worst case per assertion, Debian / Ubuntu:
111/0 against 224, 8/0 against 16, 123/0 against 160, 72/76 against 160,
73/51 against 160, 75/0 against 160 — at least 23% headroom everywhere,
and the two platforms trade places on one probe rather than one being
systematically looser.

Seven unit tests cover the helper directly: identical bitmaps, a one-pixel
shift absorbed, a three-pixel shift still reported, a colour change and
dropped content still reported at full magnitude, an outer-frame-only
difference invisible to the maximum but visible in the mean, and bitmaps
too small to have an interior compared strictly.

`/amr*` to a test-only path proxy; per vela's `specs/current/envs.md` the
legacy hostname is no longer a mapped test route and is scheduled for
decommissioning, so it must not be relied on for a compatibility redirect.

`OPEN_DESIGN_AMR_PROFILE=test` build sent every console link (dashboard,
plans, workspace settings, top-up) at a host on its way out.

Every consumer of the daemon's console origin concatenates a path onto it
(`${origin}/dashboard`, `${origin}/settings`) rather than resolving against
it as a URL base, so carrying the `/cloud` segment in the origin is safe and
mirrors the existing prod entry `https://open-design.ai/cloud`.

Left unchanged, deliberately:

  page, and prod `/amr*` still answers with a 302 to `/cloud/dashboard` that
  preserves path and query. Moving prod off the compat prefix touches a much
  wider surface and is not part of this cutover.
- feature-test still has no row in either table. Its hostname is internal and
  this repository ships publicly, so it arrives through OD_VELA_WEB_URLS /
  OD_VELA_WEB_URL at packaging time and otherwise falls back to the public
  console instead of guessing.

The daemon's public origin table had no test coverage at all; the added cases
pin the shipped test/prod/local values and the feature-test absence.

commits.commit_title: fix(strategy): refuse a turn that has nothing to design, and record why a task blocked (#7725)
commits.commit_message:
fix(strategy): refuse a turn that has nothing to design, and record why a task blocked (#7725)

* fix(daemon,web): record why a strategy task blocked, and show it

A blocked OD Next task is the one verdict a user has to act on, and
`blockedContext` is the only durable answer to "why did this stop" — the
chat error card, the diagnostics export and every later triage read it and
have nothing else to fall back on.

Three paths settle a task on `blocked`; only `blockTask` recorded anything.
`prepareStrategyRequest` computed its reason codes and returned them to its
caller without persisting them, and `finalizeStrategyPlanningResult` passed
an agent-declared `blocked` straight through, dropping the agent's own
written explanation with it. Neither logged. A field report (Design Harness
on, prototype task, answer skipped) landed on the second one: the agent
explained the stop in the user's own language, the run exited 0, and the
task reached the client with `blockedContext: null` — so the chat could only
render a fixed English "The strategy task could not continue." over an
explanation that was already on screen.

`blockedAttribution` now names that invariant and all three paths spread it,
so a fourth path cannot quietly diverge; `logStrategyTaskBlocked` gives every
block one log line. An agent-declared stop carries no machine code of its
own, and the store drops a blocked context whose reason set is empty — which
would take the agent's text down with it — so that case is named
`od_next_agent_declared_block` rather than left unattributed.

Web then prefers the recorded explanation for the error card and keeps the
fixed sentence only as the fallback for a machine gate that left no text.

Red specs first: both new daemon cases failed on the parent commit
(`blockedContext.reasonCodes` undefined), and the new web case pinned the
fixed sentence being returned regardless of what the gate recorded.

Refs OPEND-2565.

* fix(web): leave a blocked task to its own explanation

Verification found the other half of the card. Preferring the recorded
explanation put the right words on screen, but in the reported flow — ask for
a prototype, skip the discovery question — the agent had already written that
sentence into the chat as its reply. The card then restated it inside a red
"task execution failed", so a turn that had simply asked for more detail read
as a crash, twice over.

A block the agent already explained is not a failure to report: that reply is
the turn's outcome, and it is already where the user is reading. Raise no run
error for it.

Narrow on purpose. Only a Run that reached the end on its own can be spoken
for by its own output, so this needs `succeeded`; a Run that failed keeps its
error even when the agent narrated the failure, because narration is not a
substitute for the failure the user has to act on. A machine gate that blocked
without leaving any text still raises the generic error — nothing else on
screen would tell the user the task stopped, which the existing `it.each`
pins.

Refs OPEND-2565.

* fix(contracts): teach the strategy to refuse a turn it cannot design

The strategy admits a turn on the project's task type, not on what the turn
said — pick "prototype" once and every later message enters the same Full
Plan route, a greeting included. The route enum offers only direct_edit and
full_plan, both of which mean "do design work", and the clarification budget
is one round.

The prompt then taught only three outcomes: ask once, freeze a plan, deliver.
`blocked` and `canceled` appeared nowhere in it, and neither did any notion of
a request that is not a design request. So an agent handed "111" and then an
empty answer had no taught way to say "there is nothing here to build" — its
least-bad move was to invent a subject, and it did: 111 became a delivered
prototype about the number 111. The same input with the harness off gets the
sensible reply, because the ordinary route carries no obligation to deliver.

Name the refusal. The planning section now says that a greeting, an off-topic
question, a stray keystroke or a skipped answer can leave nothing to design,
that inventing a subject delivers work the user never asked for, and that the
move is to answer in visible prose and declare `outcome: blocked`. The output
contract lists every outcome and shows a blocked Runtime State, so the agent
copies it from an example instead of guessing it out of a schema enum.

No daemon change needed: `validateAcceptedTurn` branches on
clarification_required, plan_ready and completed, and imposes nothing extra on
a declared block, so this settles the task and carries the agent's own
explanation to the user through the attribution recorded earlier in this
branch.

A "not a design request" outcome of its own — one the chat could render as an
ordinary reply rather than as a block — needs the contract enum and the chat
surface, and is deliberately left to the follow-up recorded on the issue.

Refs OPEND-2589.

* fix(web): key the blocked-turn suppression on who blocked it

`main` landed its own answer here while this branch waited, and its test
refutes the rule this branch shipped. Its case is the turn right after a
question form: the agent replies "sure, three pages, here is the plan" and the
task lands blocked because that reply carried no Runtime State. The prose next
to that verdict is the agent's ordinary answer, not an account of the stop —
suppressing on the presence of text would hide a real protocol failure behind
a cheerful sentence.

So presence of text is the wrong signal; who decided to block is the right
one. Only a block the agent declared on itself can be spoken for by the
agent's own words, and that verdict already carries its own reason code from
the daemon half of this branch. Gate on the code.

The code moves to `packages/contracts` because both sides now read it: the
daemon writes it when an agent-declared block raises no machine code, and the
web reads it to tell that verdict apart from every gate the agent did not ask
for.

Both tests now hold together: `strategy-blocked-verdict.test.ts` keeps its
error for a missing Runtime State even though visible text sits beside it, and
the agent-declared block stays silent. Added the case that pins the pair.

Refs OPEND-2565.

---------
