fix(gdelt): discard partial manifest range prefixes (#8056)

## Summary

The GDELT worker can refresh intelligence when a suffix-range manifest
response starts inside a file-size field. Previously a remaining `0`
could be treated as a complete zero-size export and fail the whole run.
The HTTP range offset now establishes whether the first line is
trustworthy; at a nonzero offset that ambiguous line is discarded, while
complete descriptors and cohort checks remain strict. Byte-zero
responses retain their first entry, and missing or inconsistent range
metadata fails closed.

Railway's September 11 18:00 UTC run exited 75 after `invalid GDELT
export ZIP size: 0`; the preceding 34 observed runs completed OK. The
exact failed response was not captured, so range truncation is a
reproduced defect and likely incident cause, not a proven historical
fact. No production seeder, configuration, or Redis mutation was
performed.

## Validation

- Before repair, the new download-boundary regression failed with the
exact zero-size error. After repair, 90 focused checks pass across real
descriptor parsing, ZIP decoding, materialization, publication, consumer
cutover, country search, health and failure TTL preservation, using
controlled fixtures.
- A bounded live GCS manifest read returned HTTP 206 with matching
Content-Range and a 65,536-byte body. Its first size token was `8`; a
126-byte overlap read proved the complete token was `77108`. This
confirms the clipping mechanism without running the seeder.
- Covers zero and nonzero numeric fragments, complete zero-size
rejection at byte zero and after a prefix, missing/inconsistent range
metadata, and a prefix without a newline. Existing checksum, size,
freshness, symmetry and gap checks still pass.
- Browser/API type checks, boundary lint and `git diff --check` pass.
Focused Biome check passes with one pre-existing informational ternary
suggestion in an unchanged test.
- Sequential ce-simplify-code and ce-code-review under repository tool
mapping found no actionable issues; no independent agent or external
review automation was invoked. The country-search test initially lacked
the `tsx` loader; the corrected `node --import tsx --test` run passes

commits.commit_title: fix(rate-limit): separate a principal's API-key bucket from their session (#8060)
commits.commit_message:
fix(rate-limit): separate a principal's API-key bucket from their session (#8060)

## Summary

A paying API customer could lock themselves out of their own dashboard.
Their API key and their browser session both resolve to the same Clerk
user id, and the global limiter keyed on exactly that — so both
credentials drew from one 600/min sliding window.

This is not hypothetical. On 2026-09-11 at 17:47 UTC, for one
`api_starter` account:

| Source | Credential | Result in that minute |
|---|---|---|
| OSINT scraper | user API key | 598 × 200 |
| Dashboard (Firefox) | Clerk JWT | 2 × 200, 22 × 429 |

598 + 2 is exactly the 600 budget. The scraper consumed it, and the same
person's country deep-dive rendered with food stocks, the five-factor
scorecard, tariff trends, national debt, demographics, country
vulnerabilities and the defense industrial base all missing. The user
sees a half-empty page with no explanation.

`principalScope` now namespaces the bucket by credential —
`apikey-user:<id>` for a validated user API key, `user:<id>` for an
interactive session. The default stays `session`, so live session
buckets keep their existing key and are not reset by the rollout.

## The tradeoff, stated plainly

This separates namespaces; it does not exempt anyone. Each scope is
still capped at the same per-minute limit. The deliberate consequence is
that the aggregate a single account can spend across both credentials
doubles, from 600/min to 600 per credential.

That is the intended meter. Programmatic use is supposed to be bounded
by the plan's own `apiRateLimit` and daily allowance, which the API-key
layer already applies — but only when `API_RATE_LIMIT_ENFORCE` is on.
While it is not enforcing, `governedByApiKeyLayer` stays false and
API-key traffic falls through to this global bucket, which is how it
reached the dashboard's in the first place.

So there are two levers, and this PR only pulls the safe one. Turning on
the API-key layer is the durable fix and a config/billing decision I
deliberately have not made here.

## Why two tests

They cover two separable failures, and the second is not redundant:

- The limiter must give the two credentials independent buckets.
- The gateway must actually tell the limiter which credential was used.

Deleting both `principalScope` arguments from `gateway.ts` leaves the
limiter suite fully green. A module-only test cannot see the wiring
regress, so the gateway test asserts the invariant that any limiter call
naming a principal also names its scope — which also catches a future
third call site that forgets it.

## Validation

Written test-first. The reproduction failed in the right way before the
fix: after draining the budget through the API key, the interactive
session inherited the exhausted bucket and got a 429 instead of passing.

- Reproduction test: red before, green after.
- Rate-limit suite: 61 pass. With the sibling API-key, user-prefs and
511 suites: 92 pass.
- Gateway suites (pro-fresh-cache, cdn-origin-policy,
rpc-no-store-contract): 29 pass.
- Lint clean on all four changed files; no new typecheck errors.

Mutation-tested, three guards, each independently load-bearing:

| Mutation | Reds |
|---|---|
| Drop the gateway wiring | both wiring tests |
| Hardcode the scope to `'session'` | the branch test only |

commits.commit_title: fix(mcp): fingerprint the Pro-token gate's Sentry captures (#8058)
commits.commit_message:
fix(mcp): fingerprint the Pro-token gate's Sentry captures (#8058)

## Summary

A live Pro-MCP failure condition currently reads as drained when it is
not. On 2026-09-11, `Pro MCP token validation temporarily unavailable`
was firing in two Sentry groups at the same time: WORLDMONITOR-ZR,
resolved 2026-09-04 and quiet since, and WORLDMONITOR-T8, which took
three events that same day. Anyone looking at ZR concludes the condition
stopped. It has not.

The cause is that `api/mcp/error-fingerprint.ts` was only ever wired
into `dispatch.ts`. The two captures in `validateProMcpAuthorization`
fall back to Sentry's default stack grouping, and on the minified edge
bundle every frame is an anonymous `(vc/edge/function` with no source
map — so they collapse into the T8 catch-all, exactly the pathology that
helper's own docstring was written to close.

This also means PR #7601 does not do what its commit message says. That
PR downgraded the transient arm to `warning` so a sustained Convex
outage would "still escalate by volume." Volume split across two groups,
one of them a permanently noisy catch-all, escalates nothing. A 25-event
T8 sample held seven distinct messages across three steps and two
routes.

Both arms now carry an explicit fingerprint and stay separable from each
other: `threw` for the defect arm, `transient` for the fail-soft arm.
That preserves a distinction the surrounding comment already protects —
a thrown validator is an unexpected defect, not the fail-soft path.
Using distinct discriminators rather than leaning on the error name
means the two arms cannot merge even when the thrown error is a plain
`Error`.

## What a reviewer should expect after deploy

Sentry applies grouping at ingest, so the existing T8 and ZR groups are
untouched. New transient-verdict events will land in a **new** group
rather than in T8. That new issue appearing is the fix working, not a
regression. ZR stays resolved and should remain so, since its own
fingerprint no longer receives traffic.

Tags and levels are unchanged on both paths, so existing
`step:pro-token-validate` queries keep working.

## Validation

Written test-first against the real code path, not a source-text pin.
The test activates a throwaway DSN before importing the module, stubs
`fetch`, and asserts on the delivered Sentry envelope.

- Failing first: both arms delivered no `fingerprint` at all (`actual:
undefined`). The message and `level: warning` assertions passed in the
same run, so the harness was provably exercising the real capture rather
than silently no-opping.
- After the fix: 3/3 green.
- Neighbouring suites: 137 pass across `mcp-pro-token-fingerprint`,
`mcp-auth-entitlement-and-limits`, `mcp-error-fingerprint` and
`pro-mcp-token`; a further 206 across `mcp`, `mcp-user-key-auth` and
`mcp-billing-denial`. The pre-existing WORLDMONITOR-ZR level test still
passes.
- Mutation-tested per guard: dropping either fingerprint reds two tests;
giving both arms the same discriminator reds one.
- Lint clean on both changed files.

That mutation pass found a real weakness in my own test. The
separability assertion used `notDeepEqual` alone, which is satisfied by
`undefined !== [...]`, so it passed vacuously when a fingerprint was
missing entirely. It now asserts both fingerprints are present before
comparing them, and only then does the mutation red it.

`npm run typecheck` reports one error in `src/services/webmcp.ts`. It is
pre-existing and unrelated — I confirmed it reproduces identically on a
clean tree with this change reverted.

## Related

- Sentry: WORLDMONITOR-ZR, WORLDMONITOR-T8
- Prior art for this pattern: koala73/worldmonitor#6409,
koala73/worldmonitor#6458, koala73/worldmonitor#7228
- Level downgrade this restores the intent of: koala73/worldmonitor#7601

commits.commit_title: 🐛 fix(task-slug): keep combining marks and fall back to the instruction (#19519)
commits.commit_message:
🐛 fix(task-slug): keep combining marks and fall back to the instruction (#19519)

* 🐛 fix(task-slug): keep combining marks and fall back to the instruction

`taskTitleSlug` only allowed `\p{L}` and `\p{N}`, so scripts built on combining
marks were shredded one character at a time — `कार्य पूरा करें` became
`क-र-य-प-र-कर`, `สวัสดี` became `สว-สด`. CJK needs no marks, which is why every
existing case read as correct. Add `\p{M}`, and truncate by grapheme cluster so a
cut can neither halve a surrogate pair nor strand a mark without its base letter.

The Recent feed links a task by `COALESCE(name, instruction)` while
`useCanonicalTaskSlug` read `name` alone, so a task with only an instruction had
its slug stripped the moment the detail landed, and the copied link came out
bare. Add a shared `taskSlugTitle` helper mirroring that COALESCE (`??`, so a
name cleared to `''` still collapses the URL) and read it through store
selectors everywhere a task link is built or repaired.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KN4NTg5b1DsUgHYtsqt5zg

* 🔒 fix(task-slug): keep prompt bodies out of task URLs and bound the slug

A task's instruction is a prompt body, not a title, so it must not reach a path
segment — from there it lands in browser history, the analytics page view fired
on every history change, access logs, and anything pasted from the clipboard.
That was already true on canary for the Recent feed, which links a task by the
display title (`COALESCE(name, instruction)`); the canonicaliser happened to
strip it on arrival. Rather than making that fallback stick everywhere, drop it
from URLs entirely: `slugTitle` carries `tasks.name` alone through the Recent
payload, and the canonicaliser, the copied link and the Portal header all read
`name`. A nameless task simply has no slug, and every surface now agrees on
that instead of rewriting each other.

Grapheme counting is also not a size bound. A single cluster accepts an
unlimited run of combining marks, so `a` plus 10k accents stayed one grapheme
and produced a ~20KB segment, past what browsers and proxies accept in a
request line — and titles arrive from imported and generated content, not only
from typing. Keep whole clusters, but stop at a code-point ceiling as well.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KN4NTg5b1DsUgHYtsqt5zg

Splitting the link's slug source out of the display title left the two able to

commits.commit_title: ♻️ refactor(server): resolve the run agent config through the shared mecha rules (#19525)
commits.commit_message:
♻️ refactor(server): resolve the run agent config through the shared mecha rules (#19525)

* ♻️ refactor(server): resolve the run agent config through the shared mecha rules

`resolveRunAgentConfig` re-implemented the agent config resolution rules that `@lobechat/mecha` already owns for the client. It now gathers the snapshot from the server's sources (agent row, workspace member overrides, author-or-admin access, reply language), runs `resolveAgentConfig`, and layers only the per-call intents a run knows about: the member device override, callSubAgent chatConfig patches, the IM `/mode` override, persistence-attribution ids and the `instructions` append.

Two rule gaps closed on the shared side so both hosts agree:

- `AgentConfigResolverContext.modelOverride` carries a per-call model / provider pin (task and sub-agent spawns, explicit request overrides) into `resolveAgentModelConfig`; the runtime template renders the resolved model by default.
- Builtin system-role precedence is decided by the builtin, not the host: `RuntimeContext.storedSystemRole` hands the row's own prompt to the runtime, and the inbox (a user-editable default assistant) honors it, while feature builtins keep their runtime prompt.

Server-visible changes: regular agents now receive the reply-language instruction the client already appended; builtin runtime chatConfig merges apply; sub-agent runs keep lobe-agent and rely on its manifest resolver to hide `callSubAgent`, as the client does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(server): apply the member device override before the builtin runtime policy

Codex review: the device preference was layered after `resolveAgentConfig` had merged the builtin runtime's `agencyConfig`, so a saved `local` / `device` override replaced an onboarding runtime's `executionTarget: 'none'` and routed an internal agent to a device it disables. The override now lands on the row before the shared rules run, restoring the previous ordering where the runtime policy is merged last. Regression test covers both the builtin and the regular-agent case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(server): read the reply language for the share visitor on shared-agent runs

Codex review: `AiAgentService` is constructed as the share owner, so the locale appended to a regular agent's system role was the owner's, instructing visitor conversations to reply in the creator's language. `resolveRunAgentConfig` now takes `shareVisitorUserId` and reads the reply language for that user on share-gated runs, matching how the timezone and user info are already resolved for the visitor.

commits.commit_title: ⚡️ perf(agent): always inline agent steps in queue mode (#19531)
commits.commit_message:
⚡️ perf(agent): always inline agent steps in queue mode (#19531)

* ⚡️ perf(agent): lower the inline step start deadline to 300s

The deadline only decides whether a step may start; what keeps the
invocation alive is the headroom between it and the route's 600s
`maxDuration`. 150s of headroom was not enough in production. LLM step
length varies a lot by model, and for one family p99 is ~317s with a
~439s max. Under 450s, steps started before the deadline were observed
finishing within seconds of the kill.

300s doubles the headroom. It gives up a little of the round-trip saving
on very long operations in exchange for far fewer killed steps. A killed
step is not lost, since it resumes from the parked envelope, but it is
paid for twice.

commits.commit_title: 🐛 fix(agent): bound tool error messages so a huge tool output can't kill the operation (#19496)
commits.commit_message:
🐛 fix(agent): bound tool error messages so a huge tool output can't kill the operation (#19496)

* 🐛 fix(agent): bound tool error messages so a huge tool output can't kill the operation

A failed tool's `content` was truncated to 25k but its `error.message` was
built from the RAW output, so a command that failed with megabytes of stderr
carried all of it into the step's `nextContext` — straight into the QStash
publish body. Past the 10 MiB message quota the publish 500s
(`quota maxMessageSize exceeded`), `scheduleMessage` throws out of
`executeStep`, and the whole operation dies at the step boundary.

Seen in the wild: 120 steps / 24 minutes of real work thrown away because a
sandbox `rm -rf` hit a read-only filesystem and emitted one
`rm: cannot remove ...` line per file — 29 MB of stderr, a 29,480,903 byte
publish body.

- clamp `error.message` to 4k in `normalizeExecutionError`, independently of
  `skipResultTruncation` (that opt-out is a context budget, not a transport bound)
- guard the QStash publish itself: a body over budget gets its long strings
  clamped and logged as `agent.queue.oversized_message_clamped`, so the step
  still runs instead of taking the operation down

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): tighten the QStash body clamp until the body measures under budget

A single clamp pass only helps when the oversize comes from one runaway
string. Fragmented oversize survives it: the MCP contract keeps every raw
content block in `state`, so ~525 blocks of 20k characters each stay under the
per-string limit, pass through untouched and still publish ~10.5 MB — QStash
rejects it and the operation dies anyway.

Clamp now walks a ladder of per-string limits (25k → 4k → 512 → 0),
re-clamping the original body each rung so notices never nest, and returns the
first body that MEASURES under budget. A body that no truncation can fix
(huge in its non-string structure) now throws something diagnosable instead of
an opaque provider 500.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

⚡️ perf(agent-runtime): throttle server tools_calling stream chunks to 300ms (#19512)

* ⚡️ perf(agent-runtime): throttle server tools_calling stream chunks to 150ms

Providers stream tool-call arguments delta by delta, and every callback
carries the full accumulated call list. The server published each one
straight to the Redis stream (XADD + EXPIRE) and the Gateway, so a tool

throttle and flush the final snapshot before the step's tool lifecycle
events. Intermediate frames are safe to drop because the client replaces
the message's tools array wholesale on every chunk.

commits.commit_message:
♻️ refactor(mecha): share the context engineering core between hosts (#19514)

* ♻️ refactor(mecha): share the context engineering core between hosts

The server (`serverMessagesEngine`) and the browser (`contextEngineering`) each turned their gathered facts into `MessagesEngine` parameters by hand: the same page-agent gating, the same skills / topic-reference guards, and two diverging sets of placeholder generators. This lifts that assembly into `@lobechat/mecha` as a pure function of a typed `ContextSnapshot`:

- `agent` — the definition as it shapes the prompt (system role, identity, knowledge, history settings)
- `model` — target model and its capabilities
- `run` — the conversation plus the runtime's own flags (force finish, expertise, agent mode, step context)
- `tools` — resolved tools, skills and discovery config
- `world` — facts frozen at operation creation (mirrors `AgentState.world`)
- `step` — facts gathered per step (plan, topic references, builder / onboarding / page state)
- `variables` — host-resolved placeholder values that override the core's leak guards

`buildMessagesEngineParams(snapshot)` produces the engine parameters; `runContextEngineering(snapshot)` runs the engine; `createVariableGenerators` owns the timezone-localized temporal placeholders and the device leak guards. The server's `serverMessagesEngine` becomes a thin adapter (`toContextSnapshot`) over its existing parameter type, so the per-step builder is untouched and behaves identically; the browser follows in the next PR.

♻️ refactor(agent-runtime): carve principal, plan and host slots out of state.metadata (#19513)

Third and last step of the state restructure (#19498 world/binding, #19505 origin). The remaining creation-time facts in `state.metadata` fall into three business groups, each now a typed slot on `AgentState`:

- `principal` — under whose authority the run acts and what it may do: `actor.{shareVisitor, bot, deviceScope}`, `policy.deviceAccess`, `audit.{clientIp, userAgent}`. Decided at creation and re-presented, never re-derived, at each dispatch boundary.

- `host` — what the host needs to deliver and retry the run: `hooks` (serialized webhook configs) and `queue.{retries, retryDelay}`. Carried by the runtime without interpretation.

`ExecutionPlan` / `ExecutionPlanUnroutedReason` move to `@lobechat/types` so the runtime can type the slot; `src/helpers/executionTarget` re-exports them. `normalizeAgentState` lifts the legacy keys on load and folds a legacy `metadata.modelRuntimeConfig` into the top-level slot when it is absent. `HookDispatcher.dispatch` accepts the wire-shape `SerializedAgentHook[]` the slot carries and narrows to `SerializedHook` itself; `isAgentShareRun` takes the state; `resolveRunActiveDeviceId` / `resolveRunProjectSkills` read `plan` and `principal`; the dynamic intervention resolvers receive the plan's working directory alongside the ledger.

`metadata` is now the run ledger only: what the runtime and host write while the operation executes.

commits.commit_title: ✨ feat(goal): let the system planner lead and hand problems to the main Agent (#19477)
commits.commit_message:
✨ feat(goal): let the system planner lead and hand problems to the main Agent (#19477)

* ✨ feat(goal): let the system planner lead and hand problems to the main Agent

Configuring a main Agent used to replace the coordinator's own planning. `tick`
asked it first and returned early, so on a Goal that had both, the exploration
planner never got a turn — and `goal.create` rejected the combination outright
("Manager mode owns initial and subsequent planning").

The two are layers, not rivals, and the split is visible in their vocabularies.
Exploration says `expand | revise | verify`: it can move within the graph but
cannot express "this goal is mis-framed", "the judge was wrong" or "stop and ask".
A main Agent says `tasks | verify | retry | escalate`, which is the supervisory
half. Meanwhile the main Agent was only ever consulted about failures that passed
the transport whitelist, so a Goal could park on its owner for hours with a main
Agent configured and idle.

Invert the order:

- The system planner owns the ordinary path. With exploration configured, `advance`
  only settles a turn already in flight — a turn already paid for has to land —
  and starts no new one. A Goal whose only planner is the main Agent is still led
  by it.
- `gateOrTakeOver` replaces the three `openFailureDecision` call sites. Every
  stop-on-a-person funnels through there, and the coordinator only reaches it once
  its own policy is out of moves: the failure matched no recovery branch, the
  attempt budget ran out, or the reason could not be classified. That is exactly
  the class the deterministic lane cannot express, so it is handed over. The ladder
  is supervision, then the main Agent, then the Gate.
- An invited turn skips the "is there unfinished work" and "is this a recognised
  transport failure" narrowings. Those ask whether an *uninvited* turn should
  interrupt running work; the caller has already answered a harder question. Turn
  limits, budgets and the compare-and-swap claim still hold.
- An invited turn with no turn budget left declines instead of pausing the Goal, so
  the Gate keeps carrying the real question instead of "the main Agent is out of
  turns".
- The create-time exclusivity check is gone: exploration, supervision and seed
  tasks may now accompany a main Agent. Ordering resolves what exclusivity did.

Prompt cohort goes to v4: a takeover turn is told which problem it inherited and
that the Goal stops on a person without it, so `escalate` means "a human really is
required" rather than being the only reachable answer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(goal): keep supervision first and turn a takeover escalation into its Gate

Two P1s from Codex review, both caused by the combinations this PR newly allows.

**Supervision was losing its place in the ladder.** With `manager` + `supervision`
and no `exploration`, `mayStartTurn` is true, so an uninvited turn claimed a
recognised transport failure at the top of `tick` and returned early —
`decideNextMove` never reached `failure_decision`, and `reviewFailure` never ran.
That reverses the documented order, spends a planning turn on a failure the
supervisor recovers by itself, and skips the supervisor's stricter
actor-authored-status check. An uninvited turn now stands down from failures
entirely when supervision is enabled; whatever the supervisor declines arrives at
`gateOrTakeOver`, which invites the Agent properly.

**An escalation had nothing to escalate to.** The takeover contract says
`escalate` puts the Gate back one turn later, but the escalate branch only paused
the Goal and recorded a status event — no Decision, no answerable question, and
every later tick sat on `goal_paused`. An escalation from a takeover turn no longer
touches the Goal's status, so the next tick reaches the same handover point; there
`takeOver` declines a problem its own escalation already answered and the Gate
opens, carrying the Agent's reason in the question. An ordinary planning turn's
escalation still pauses, because nothing is holding a Gate behind it.

`managerState.problem` records what a turn was invited for. It is what separates a
takeover turn from ordinary planning, and what keeps the same problem from being
handed over twice.

Both regressions are pinned: reverting either fix turns its test red.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(goal): let a takeover commit the moves it was offered, keyed per task

Codex review round 2. Both findings are the takeover contract promising more than
the code accepts.

**Three of the four advertised actions could not commit.** `submit` refuses `tasks`
and `verify` whenever any task node is unfinished — which a takeover's inherited
task always is — and `retry` is refused for anything outside the transport
whitelist. So the prompt offered four moves and only `escalate` could ever land.
The unfinished-work guard exists to stop an *uninvited* turn from double planning
the frontier; a takeover's inherited work is stuck by definition, which is why it
was handed over, so a corrective task is the answer rather than the thing to
forbid. The guard is now waived for an invited turn, and the prompt stops
advertising a retry for failures that will be refused.

**The already-answered key was too coarse.** "Task attempt budget was exhausted" is
the same sentence for every task that reaches it, so keying on the reason alone let
a second task skip its own takeover and inherit the first task's diagnosis in its
gate — resolving the first gate does not clear `managerState`. The key is now task
and reason together, through a shared `problemKey` so the writer and the reader
cannot drift.

While there: any committed plan now counts as an answer, not just `escalate`. If
the Agent's move did not unstick the Goal, handing the same problem back buys the
same move; the Gate is the honest next step and the Agent's reasoning rides on it.

Both regressions are pinned: reverting either fix turns its test red.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(goal): retire the work a takeover plan replaces

Codex review round 3, and it is right that the previous fix only moved the wall.
Accepting `tasks` and `verify` on an invited turn changed validation and nothing
else: the inherited task node stayed nonterminal, so the next tick's frontier
reached that older blocked node before the freshly created corrective node and
routed straight back to `failure_decision`, while terminal verification could not
start at all while it was unfinished. The advertised actions committed and the Goal
still fell through to the human Gate.

A `tasks` or `verify` plan from a takeover turn now retires the node it inherited.
That is the same move the Gate offers a person under "Retire task", scoped to the
single node this turn was invited about, attributed to the main Agent, and only
reachable on an invited turn. It abandons a direction rather than re-spending on
it, so it stays clear of the open question about who may pay for another attempt.

`managerState.problemTaskId` carries the blocked task alongside the dedupe key, so
the node is found without parsing a composite string whose reason half is free
text.

Pinned: the test ticks past the submission and asserts the replaced node is retired
and the Goal does not land on a Gate. Reverting the retire turns it red.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(goal): hand a failed terminal acceptance to the main Agent too

Codex review round 4, and it is the same species as the previous three: a guard
written for uninvited turns sitting above the invited branch.

`startTurn` returns null whenever a terminal acceptance task exists on the graph.
That rule means "verification exists, stop planning more work", which is right for
an uninvited turn and exactly wrong for a takeover invited BECAUSE the terminal
acceptance is the thing that failed. So a Goal with a main Agent configured still
reached a bare human Gate on the one failure where a second opinion matters most.
The guard now lives inside the uninvited branch with the others.

The retirement added in the previous commit deliberately does NOT apply to the
acceptance node. `decideWithoutFrontier` finds that task by TITLE regardless of
status, so retiring it parks the Goal on `no_progress` with neither a Gate nor a
verdict — and failing the Goal is the Gate's own `retire` answer, coupled to that
option rather than to the node's status. A takeover on a failed acceptance can
therefore diagnose an incorrect judge and put that reasoning on the Gate, or plan
corrective work; making corrective work supersede a failed acceptance by itself
needs the acceptance lifecycle to allow superseding, and that is a separate change.
Both limits are stated in the README rather than left for the next reviewer.

Pinned: one test asserts the takeover starts for a failed acceptance with no Gate
opened, another asserts the acceptance node is never retired. Reverting either half
turns its test red.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(goal): refuse takeover plans that would strand the graph

Codex review round 5. Two of its three findings are defects in what the previous
commits shipped; the third is a real gap that this PR does not close, and the README
now says so instead of leaving it for the next reviewer.

**Retiring a node something depends on strands the dependent.** A prerequisite counts
as met only when it is `resolved`, so a retired predecessor blocks its dependents
forever and the Goal lands on `no_frontier`. Rewiring them onto the replacement would
be the answer, but the graph model has no edge removal, so the old `depends_on` edge
would keep pointing at the retired node. Retirement is refused when the stuck node has
dependents, and that block goes to the Gate.

**A failed Goal acceptance cannot be superseded, so stop accepting plans that try.**
The acceptance task is matched by TITLE regardless of status: a corrective task returns
to the same failed node, and `verify` sets `readyForAcceptance` without producing a
fresh run. Both submissions used to be accepted and then strand. `tasks` and `verify`
are now refused for an acceptance takeover, and the prompt names that limit together
with the dependents one, so the offer and the answer are the same sentence and a turn
is not spent discovering the difference.

**Not closed: exploration's own stop conditions.** The experiment limit, a spent
revision allowance and a planner error all pause the Goal directly rather than passing
through `gateOrTakeOver`, and `eligible()` then rejects the paused Goal — so the
planner whose "out of moves" most deserves a second opinion never reaches the main
Agent. Closing it requires an invited turn to revive a Goal the system paused, which
changes who may restart one; that belongs with the open question about who may pay for
another attempt, not in this PR.

Both fixes are pinned: reverting either turns its test red.

commits.commit_message:
♻️ refactor(agent-runtime): carve typed world/binding slots out of state.metadata (#19498)

* ♻️ refactor(agent-runtime): carve typed world/binding slots out of state.metadata

Every reader of the prompt-side run context (agent config, group roster, project instructions, connector note, user memory/timezone, search decision, channel facts, eval context) and of the device binding (active device id/platform/system info) used to reach into the untyped `state.metadata` bag, so a value that was not spelled out in the creation-time field list silently disappeared.

`AgentState` now carries two typed slots derived from what those fields mean:

- `world` — what the model is told about the run's world. Frozen at operation creation; the context engine only reads it.
- `binding` — late-bound execution facts. The one business slot the host may rewrite at a step boundary (`computeDeviceContext`).

`normalizeAgentState` lifts the legacy metadata keys into the slots at the persistence boundary (Redis + in-memory state load) so blobs written before this change keep working, without carrying the data twice. `RuntimeExecutorContext` drops its per-field copies; readers go through `state.world` / `state.binding`, and `resolveRunActiveDeviceId` takes the state instead of the metadata bag.

* ♻️ refactor(agent-runtime): read the trace header model from world.agent

* ♻️ refactor(agent-runtime): declare the search decision shape instead of importing model-bank

The runtime package should not take a dependency on the model catalog for one five-field interface. `SearchDecisionSnapshot` is declared next to the world slot and is structurally identical to the `model-bank` resolver output, so the server keeps passing its value unchanged.

commits.commit_title: ⚡️ perf(agent): run consecutive agent steps in one invocation (#19470)
commits.commit_message:
⚡️ perf(agent): run consecutive agent steps in one invocation (#19470)

* ⚡️ perf(agent): run consecutive steps in one invocation

Every step boundary cost a full queue round-trip: ~2.9s at p50 across
production traces, with nothing under 2s. That is 13.6% of all agent-run
wall time, plus another 8.4% for the same hop before step 0, and it rises
past a quarter of wall time on multi-step operations.

The QStash worker now keeps stepping inside one invocation for as long as
the operation has a next step ready and its time budget allows. Past the
budget the pending step goes back to the queue and a fresh invocation
picks it up, so the tail behaves exactly as it does today.

- `executeStep` takes `inlineContinuation` and hands the next step back as
  a `continuation` instead of publishing it. Every terminal outcome and
  every park (waiting_for_human, pending approval, async-tool wait) leaves
  it absent, so the loop stops on its own without special-casing them.
- One lock owner spans the whole loop. The operation lock is now re-entrant
  for the owner that already holds it; owner tokens carry a random UUID, so
  a redelivery from the queue still loses the race. The lock is no longer
  dropped and re-claimed at each boundary.
- Only the first step carries the delivery's one-shot payload. Inlined
  steps must not replay a human input or an approval that already ran.
- The existing `stepCount > stepIndex` stale-delivery guard already covers
  a redelivery arriving after the loop advanced past its step.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🔧 chore(agent): set the inline step deadline to 450s

Leaves ~150s of headroom under the route's 600s maxDuration, which covers
the p99 LLM step (~125s), so a step that starts just under the deadline
still finishes inside the invocation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): park the inline step envelope so a dead loop can recover

Codex review caught a failure mode the loop introduced. Today a worker
that dies mid-step recovers: state never advanced, so QStash redelivers
the same step and it runs again. With the loop, a worker that dies during
step N+2 leaves state at N+2 while the only queued message is still the
original step N. The `stepCount > stepIndex` stale-delivery guard ACKs
that redelivery, and the operation is stranded with nothing queued.

The loop deliberately does not publish the next step, so the envelope it
would have published is parked in Redis instead, written before the step
runs. A redelivery that lands behind a parked envelope resumes from the
envelope rather than from its own (older) index, which is the same
recovery the queue used to provide.

- `agent_runtime_inline_resume:{operationId}` holds the envelope under the
  existing 2h operation TTL, and is dropped with the other operation keys.
- Cleared when a step ends without a continuation, and when the deadline
  hands the pending step back to the queue — in both cases something else
  owns the next step and a lingering pointer could re-run it.
- A resumed run carries none of the delivery's one-shot payload: it stands
  in for a later iteration of the dead loop, not for the original message.
- Read failures degrade to null; without an envelope the handler just runs
  the step it was given.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): fall back to the queue when the inline envelope can't be parked

`saveInlineResume` swallowed its Redis error, so a failed park still
inlined the next step — with no envelope and no queue message behind it,
which is exactly the stranding the envelope exists to prevent.

It now reports failure and inlining is conditional on the park succeeding.
When Redis is unavailable the step takes the ordinary queue round-trip:
one step boundary slower, but the recovery path stays intact.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ✨ feat(agent): gate the inline step loop behind a runtime feature flag

Makes the loop a rollout switch rather than a deploy-time behaviour change,
so it can be turned on for a slice of traffic and turned off again without
shipping anything.

Uses the existing RuntimeConfig path rather than a new mechanism: the flag
`inline_agent_steps` joins `FeatureFlagsSchema`, resolves through
`getServerFeatureFlagsStateFromRuntimeConfig` (Redis-backed, ~5s in-process
cache), and accepts either a boolean or a user-ID allowlist like `dev_dock`
and `agent_share` do. Develop Center already writes that snapshot.

Default is off, so merging and deploying this changes nothing until the
flag is published.

- The gate fails closed: any error resolving it falls back to one step per
  delivery.
- Looking up a parked envelope is deliberately NOT gated. Operations that
  were mid-loop when the flag flipped off have an envelope and nothing
  queued behind them, so ignoring it would strand exactly the runs a
  rollback is meant to protect.
- Envelope clearing moves from `executeStep` to the handler, which is the
  only place that knows the invocation is done with it — including the
  flag-off resume path, which `executeStep` no longer sees as inline.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): keep the retry count and surface envelope read failures

Two more findings from Codex review, both about the inline loop's recovery
path silently turning a retryable delivery into a dead end.

Preserve `externalRetryCount` when resuming from a parked envelope. A step
that parked for approval but failed to persist its Review is only replayed
while the count is nonzero (`shouldReplayPendingInterventionLifecycle`).
The resume path dropped it along with the one-shot payload, so the stale
guard ACKed the step and the approval never became available. The count
describes the delivery, not the step's payload, so it belongs on both paths.

Surface a failed envelope read instead of reporting "no envelope". The two
have opposite consequences: absent means run the delivered step, unreadable
may mean an operation is mid-loop with nothing queued behind it. Collapsing
them ACKed that delivery as stale and stranded the run. The read now
propagates and the queue retries.

An unparseable envelope stays non-fatal — retrying cannot fix it, so it is
reported and treated as absent rather than looping into the DLQ. Clearing
stays best-effort: a stale envelope only resumes a step ahead of the
delivered index, and the next park overwrites it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): only redirect plain step deliveries to a parked envelope

Self-review finding. The envelope lookup keyed purely on
`parked.stepIndex > stepIndex`, regardless of what the delivery carried.

That silently rewrites deliveries that exist for their own reason —
approvals, async-tool resumes, barrier probes, member-timeout watchdogs —
into ordinary step runs with their payload dropped. The group-member
timeout is the sharp edge: `scheduleGroupMemberTimeout` publishes it on the
member operation at `stepIndex: 0`, so ANY envelope is "ahead" of it. A
member that is mid-loop always has one, so the watchdog would be swallowed
and the parked supervisor would wait forever.

It compounds: the hijacked delivery then loses the lock race against the
loop that is still running, and on its way out clears that loop's envelope
— removing the recovery pointer from a live operation.

The lookup is now skipped entirely unless the delivery is a plain "run the
next step" message, which also saves a Redis read on every watchdog and
intervention delivery.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): clear the inline envelope only while holding the lock

Codex review. Clearing was an unconditional DEL on the operation's envelope
key, which lets a worker delete a pointer it does not own.

A redelivery can read envelope k, stall while the active worker finishes k
and parks k+1, then lose the lock race and be told its step is stale. On the
way out it cleared the key — deleting the live worker's newer envelope. If
that worker then died during k+1, its own redelivery would hit the stale
guard with no pointer to resume from, stranding the operation.

Ownership of the operation lock is the right predicate: whoever holds it is
the worker whose envelope this is. Clearing is now a two-key Lua compare
against the lock's owner token, mirroring the existing release script, so a
worker that lost the race no-ops instead of deleting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

commits.commit_title: ♻️ refactor(context-engine): let the engine assemble the system message (#19485)
commits.commit_message:
♻️ refactor(context-engine): let the engine assemble the system message (#19485)

* ♻️ refactor(context-engine): let the engine assemble the system message

The server composed the final system prompt by string-appending onto
`agentConfig.systemRole` from three files across the pipeline: the resolver,
`operationPrep` (project instructions), and `toolDiscovery` (borrowed-connector
attribution). That is why the resolved config had to stay mutable all the way
through, and why each append site carried a comment vouching for the aliasing —
"appending here still reaches the LLM because `createOperation` reads
`agentConfig` below". Correctness depended on nobody cloning the object, which
the `do not clone` warning enforced by convention rather than by type.

The mechanism for doing this properly already existed and was being bypassed.
`BaseSystemRoleProvider` is purpose-built — subclasses return content, the base
finds or creates the system message and joins with `\n\n` — and the engine has a
declared "Phase 2: System Message Assembly" where a dozen injectors already use
it.

So the two late contributions become injectors. `ProjectInstructionsInjector`
takes the files rather than a rendered block, because wrapping them is
presentation and belongs to whoever owns the system message.
`ConnectorOwnershipInjector` takes a rendered note, because naming the
authorizers needs a user lookup the engine cannot perform — the same split
`EvalContextSystemInjector` makes with `envPrompt`.

Both run immediately after `SystemRoleInjector`, which is exactly where their
text used to land. Placing them later would silently reorder the prompt behind
every other Phase 2 provider; keeping the position keeps it byte-identical.

The data reaches the engine on `AgentConfigWithId`, which already carries
run-scoped fields stamped by one stage for another (`subAgentChatConfigOverride`).
Same transport as before, structured payload instead of a concatenated string —
no new plumbing through the state blob, and no size change, since the same text
already travelled inside `systemRole`.

Not included: the persona-level appends inside the resolver (builtin runtime
role, page/task agent, per-call instructions). Those compose what the agent IS,
which the resolve phase owns; these two are run context, which the engine owns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ♻️ refactor(agent): carry system-message context on the operation, not the config

Follow-up to the previous commit, which moved the two late system-prompt
contributions into context-engine injectors but carried their payloads on
`AgentConfigWithId`. That was the same category error in a better shape: it
removed the string concatenation and kept smuggling run context through the
agent's configuration. Project instructions come from the workspace and the
connector note from tool discovery — neither is part of what the agent IS.

They now travel the way every other piece of run context does. There is an
established family of them on the operation metadata — `agentShareVisitor`,
`botContext`, `botPlatformContext`, `discordContext`, `userTimezone`,
`evalContext` — each mapped onto `RuntimeExecutorContext` and consumed
downstream, and `evalContext` in particular already feeds an injector.

`expertise` is the exact precedent and this follows it end to end:
`prepareOperation` and `discoverTools` return the values instead of mutating
the config, `startOperation` puts them on the operation, `createOperation`
persists them into `state.metadata`, `AgentRuntimeService` maps them onto the
executor context, and the context builder reads them from there.

Persisting matters rather than being incidental: steps can be claimed by
different workers, so anything the engine needs has to survive on the
operation. `createOperation` builds `state.metadata` from an explicit field
list, so a value not named there is dropped without a word — the same shape of
trap as the zod schema that silently stripped `createdAt`.

The two fields added to `AgentConfigWithId` in the previous commit are removed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent): forward the system-message context, and restore its order

Two from review, and the first one meant the whole change was dead on the
server.

`serverMessagesEngine` destructures a fixed parameter list, so the two new
fields never reached `MessagesEngine` and both injectors always saw
`undefined`. The old concatenation was already gone, so every server run would
have lost its project instructions and connector attribution outright —
`AGENTS.md` silently absent from the prompt. Neither the injector unit tests
nor the type checker caught it: the tests exercised the injectors directly,
and the call site passes an intermediate object, which disables
excess-property checking.

So the regression test lives at the wrapper-to-engine seam, not on the
injectors. Verified it fails without the forwarding.

The injector order was also wrong. `discoverTools` runs before
`prepareOperation`, so the old appends produced persona → connector note →
project instructions; the injectors had them the other way round, against an
adjacent comment claiming the prompt was byte-identical. Connector attribution
now precedes the project instructions, with a test pinning it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ✅ test(agent): cover every link the system-message context travels

The forwarding bug shipped with green injector tests because they exercised
the injectors directly. The wrapper test added with the fix only covers the
last link; a value dropped anywhere earlier is just as silent and just as
total.

Every failure this feature has had — the wrapper's fixed parameter list, and
`createOperation` assembling `state.metadata` from an explicit field list —
was a name missing from a list rather than broken logic. Nothing about that
shape surfaces in behaviour: the injectors keep working, they simply never
receive anything. So each link now has an assertion of its own, and each was
verified to fail with its forwarding removed:

  createOperation params → state.metadata   (AgentRuntimeService.test)
  executor context       → engine input     (serverCallLlmContextBuilder.test)
  engine input           → system message   (serverMessagesEngine.test)

One link is still covered by reading rather than by a test: `state.metadata` →
executor context. And a true end-to-end run through `execAgent` is
disproportionately expensive here, because the project instructions originate
in the device workspace-scan path — reaching them needs an activeDeviceId, a
device row and a scan result, none of which is the thing under test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ✅ test(agent): pin the stage order the system message depends on

Drives the real `execAgent` pipeline and asserts that tool discovery runs
before operation prep. That order is the reason connector attribution precedes
the project instructions in the assembled system message, and until now it
rested on a comment citing two line numbers — the same kind of claim that was
wrong the first time this ordering was written down.

Carrying a real payload end to end through this harness turned out to cost
more than it returns. The project instructions originate in the device
workspace-scan path, so reaching them needs an active device, a device row, a
fresh cached scan, and the agent-skill lookup that happens to share the same
`try` — each mock revealing the next, and none of it the thing under test. The
payload is therefore covered link by link instead, which also matches the
failure shape: every regression it has had was a name missing from an explicit
field list, not broken logic.

Worth recording separately: project instructions and the project skill lookup
share one `try`, so a skill-model failure silently drops the instructions too.
Pre-existing, unrelated to this change, and not fixed here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

commits.commit_title: ♻️ refactor(mecha): extract agent config resolution into a shared package (#19476)
commits.commit_message:
♻️ refactor(mecha): extract agent config resolution into a shared package (#19476)

There are two Mecha layers doing the same job against different data sources.
The browser assembles an agent's effective run config in
`src/services/chat/mecha` (~2300 lines including its context builder); the
server assembles the same thing in `apps/server/src/modules/Mecha` plus an
851-line `serverCallLlmContextBuilder` that inlines the resolution alongside
reads of six database models. Both wrap the same shared `MessagesEngine`, and
the primitives underneath (`getActivePluginIds`, `ToolResolver`,
`resolveTopicReferences`) were extracted long ago — only the orchestration
above them was left duplicated.

Spot-checked rather than inferred from size: both sides independently compute
`enabledToolIds`, `enabledManifests` and the merged `systemRole` from an agent
config, producing the same shape from different sources.

This moves the browser's resolution rules into `@lobechat/mecha` unchanged,
behind an `AgentConfigSnapshot` of everything they previously read from
Zustand. The browser now gathers that snapshot — 76 lines — and delegates.
Nothing else changes: the barrel re-exports the same names, so no call site
moved, and `getTargetAgentId` stays behind because it reads the active agent.

The package takes the name both hosts already use for this layer, because the
rest of it follows: context engineering, tool composition and model-parameter
resolution are duplicated the same way and belong in the same home. A resolver
is the first inhabitant, not the whole tenancy.

It is a package of its own rather than part of `@lobechat/agent-runtime`
because the runtime keeps exactly three runtime dependencies — everything
heavy is type-only — and that is what let the CLI adopt it. These rules need
`builtin-agents`, which alone pulls in eight builtin-tool packages. Folding
them in would invert the property that makes the runtime portable. The runtime
also never resolves config; it reads `state.metadata.agentConfig` as an opaque
cast for a single field, so resolution belongs to the host that starts it.

`canManage` is an input rather than something the rules compute. The browser
answers it from the cache its picker populates and the server from
`isResourceAuthorOrAdmin`, which is asynchronous — a seam that only works if
the decision arrives already made.

Behaviour is pinned by the existing suite: all 77 of
`agentConfigResolver.test.ts` pass untouched, and they mock the stores, so they
exercise the new gathering and the extracted rules end to end. The package also
has its own suite that builds the snapshot by hand and never mocks a store, so
a store read creeping back in fails there even while the client tests still
pass.

The server and a device adopt this in later PRs — one host at a time, so a
regression stays attributable. For the device the payoff is the point: its
context port stops being an 851-line problem and becomes a snapshot to fill.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.commit_title: 💄 style(acceptance): name the author on the record and drop the shared-link banner (#19478)
commits.commit_message:
💄 style(acceptance): name the author on the record and drop the shared-link banner (#19478)

* 💄 style(acceptance): name the author on the record and drop the shared-link banner

The acceptance header now carries who delivered the work, the way a pull
request names its author: avatar and name sit right after the status, ahead
of the counts. `getBundle` resolves that profile from the acceptance's own
owner, so a visitor holding nothing but the shared link still sees whose
record they are reading.

With the name on the record, the standing "shared with you" banner had
nothing left to say that the page did not already show, so it is gone —
component, both mount points, and its five locale keys.

The per-check entry beside the status was a small button wearing a 44px
floor, which drew it as a block twice the height of the row it lives on.
Dropping the override lets it sit inline at its own size.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 💄 style(acceptance): lead the header with the delivery's name, then one bar

Review feedback on the first round: the title should come before the status,
the pass/uncertain tally beside it should go, and the origin chips sitting on
their own row underneath should join the same bar.

So the name leads, and one bar under it carries state, author, the origin
agent, the originating conversation, the pull request, and the per-check
entry. The header goes from three rows to two.

The tally and the last-run time are dropped outright. They change every round
and read as a verdict while sitting above the checklist that actually shows
them, so `acceptance.verdict.latestAt` goes with them.

With both avatars now side by side in one bar, an origin agent without a
picture drew the component's "UN" placeholder next to a real face. It falls
back to its own initial, the way the author's does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 💄 style(acceptance): trail the title with the per-check entry, on hover

Review feedback on the second round: the entry reads cleaner after the name
than inside the meta bar, and it only needs to be there when reached for.

So it moves out of the bar to sit after the title, and fades in when the row
is hovered. It fades rather than hides: an entry that appears by reflow would
retitle the row under the pointer, and `visibility: hidden` drops the button
from the tab order and the accessibility tree, which was measurable — with it,
`btn.focus()` left `document.activeElement` elsewhere and the `:focus-within`
rule could never fire. `pointer-events` keeps the faded box from swallowing
clicks meant for the title. Touch never hovers, and the button already removes
itself below the mobile breakpoint, so nothing is stranded there.

commits.commit_title: ✨ feat(agent-runtime): default extensible agent loop with an explicit stop reason (#19153)
commits.commit_message:
✨ feat(agent-runtime): default extensible agent loop with an explicit stop reason (#19153)

Three hosts drive this runtime and each wrote its own loop: the server's
`executeSync`, the browser's `streamingExecutor`, and the package example. A
fourth is coming for device-hosted runs. They have drifted.

The server breaks explicitly on `interrupted`, on a parked status, and on
`shouldContinueExecution` — a private method that is the only complete
statement of the rules, covering cost limits and a missing next context. The
browser loops on `status !== 'done' && status !== 'error'` and escapes a
parked run only because its steps happen to return no next context. The two
agree today by coincidence, not by design: whoever changes what a parked step
returns will make the browser take another turn on a parked state.

`runAgentLoop` owns exactly two things — when to stop, and what context the
next step receives. It takes the step as a parameter rather than calling
`runtime.step` itself, because a step means very different things per host: on
the server it claims a distributed lock, persists state, dispatches hooks and
records a trace; in the browser and on a device it is a direct `runtime.step`.
Collapsing those is how a shared loop becomes something every host works
around, so persistence, hooks, streaming and quota deliberately stay outside.

The stop reason is the part worth having. Every host re-derived it after the
fact — the server to decide whether to emit `max_steps` completion signals,
the browser to choose between a terminal lifecycle event and the parked one.
Computed once, it cannot drift.

Migrating the example surfaced a real distinction: "no next context" describes
what a step PRODUCED, so it cannot be asked before the first step. A run may
legitimately open with no context, and checking it up front would end every
loop before it began. Hence `resolveTerminalReason` (status and cost, safe
before any step) alongside the full `resolveStopReason`.

No host is migrated here. The server's per-step distributed path — where
`executeStep` is scheduled and re-entered rather than looped — is NOT a loop
and must not adopt this; only its `executeSync` should, and separately, so a
regression is attributable.

commits.commit_title: 🐛 fix(verify): stop the acceptance review from rejecting evidence it never saw (#19468)
commits.commit_message:
🐛 fix(verify): stop the acceptance review from rejecting evidence it never saw (#19468)

* 🐛 fix(verify): share the review evidence budget so one attachment cannot starve the rest

The review predictor spent its 60k-character text budget in capture order and
broke out of the loop once it ran dry, so a large attachment silently consumed
everything behind it. On a real Goal delivery the four rows were 31,853
characters of script source, a 4,307-character rerun log, a 52,226-character
score dump and a 1,319-character summary: the summary never reached the prompt
at all, and the reviewer rejected the check for missing evidence that had in
fact been attached.

Allocate by water-filling instead — walk the rows smallest first and grant each
an equal share of what is still unspent, so every row is guaranteed
`budget / rowCount` characters and small rows stay whole.

Two related gaps in the same block:

- A text row's own description was dropped, while visual rows had always carried
  theirs. The caption is often the only thing that says what a payload is
  ("rerun log, byte-identical to round 1"), so the reviewer was left inferring
  from raw bytes.
- Truncation was applied silently. A payload that stops mid-line reads as a
  corrupt artifact, which invites exactly the "insufficient evidence" rejection
  the truncation caused. Truncation and omission are now stated in the text.

The allocation moved to its own module so the rule is testable without a
database; content resolution for every candidate row now happens before
allocation, which is the cost of being able to size them fairly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ✨ feat(verify): let the acceptance review report a criterion it cannot decide

The automated review only had `accept` and `reject`, so "this delivery fell
short" and "no reader could settle this check" were the same answer. Criteria
that ask the reviewer to act on the system — rerun the delivered scripts, build
the project, drive something live — are undecidable from captured evidence by
construction, and the hardened v3 prompt correctly turns "no affirmative proof"
into a reject. The result is a Goal Task that re-delivers the same artifacts
against the same unprovable criterion until its attempt budget runs out.

Add `unjudgeable` as a third verdict:

- The prompt defines it by one test: could some capture the builder is able to
  produce settle this check? If yes it is a reject and the comment says what to
  capture. Only if no capture could ever settle it is it `unjudgeable`. Thin,
  blank, truncated or unconvincing evidence stays a reject, so this is not an
  escape hatch from the leniency the prompt was hardened against.
- `reviewGoalDelivery` keeps it out of the rejected bucket and aggregates by
  precedence rather than last-writer-wins, since checks are judged concurrently.
  A genuine rejection outranks it: one short check still makes another attempt
  worth paying for.
- A task whose review could not decide pauses with a new contract string that
  deliberately has NO recovery branch, so the coordinator routes it to a person
  on the first occurrence instead of buying another identical attempt.

The action vocabulary lives twice — the model's JSON schema and the column it is
stored in — so a test now pins the two lists to each other. The column enum is
type-level only in drizzle, so no migration is needed.

`REVIEW_PREDICT_PROMPT_VERSION` goes to v4 because agreement statistics are
grouped by (provider, model, promptVersion); the new cohort covers both this
change and the evidence-budget change it ships with. Existing v3 rows stay
attributable, and open acceptances re-judge on the next request.

Out of scope, stated for the reviewer: the acceptance page still renders no card
for an `unjudgeable` prediction (only rejects surface), and nothing yet escalates
such a check to a judge that can execute.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(verify): name the trigger that makes a criterion undecidable

Probing the pinned review model on a criterion that explicitly reads "the
reviewer must log in and compare the memory curve themselves", the model still
answered `reject` with "no monitoring evidence attached" — it read an action it
cannot perform as evidence somebody forgot to capture.

Naming the trigger fixes it: a criterion that makes the REVIEWER the actor
cannot be settled by any capture, because the reviewer cannot become that actor.
Verified against gemini-3.6-flash: that criterion now returns `unjudgeable`,
while a check whose evidence is merely absent still returns `reject`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(verify): tell the review which artifacts it was not shown

The review request silently carries less than the check does: frames past
`MAX_VISUALS` are dropped, audio and video are never read, and a text row whose
payload cannot be resolved simply vanishes. The prompt then demands affirmative
proof, so the model answers "not observable in the evidence" about artifacts that
exist and were withheld from it — and the comment tells the builder to recapture
something already captured.

Driven against a real check that carries five verification screenshots, with the
pinned review model and the real frames:

| Withheld declared | Run 1 | Run 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no (current behaviour) | reject: "缺少单元 U208 和 U223 的截图原图" | reject, same two units |
| yes | accept | accept |

Both rejections name precisely the two frames the request itself removed.

Declare them instead. `describeWithheldEvidence` lists what the request held back
— frames past the cap, media this reviewer cannot open, payloads it could not
resolve — with each artifact's own caption, because the caption is the only handle
the model has on something it cannot open. The prompt gains one rule: a withheld
artifact is never cited as missing, and a verdict that turns on one is
`unjudgeable` rather than a reject.

The caveat is also persisted on the judged row. "Rejected having seen everything"
and "rejected while two frames were held back" are otherwise the same verdict in
the agreement statistics, which is exactly the distinction the review-quality work
needs. `status_reason` is redocumented to cover that.

Scope on this account's labelled history: 50 of 1861 checks carried more frames
than the request attaches, and 6 carried audio or video the reviewer never reads.

One read of the check's evidence now feeds all three decisions — which frames to
attach, which payloads to inline, and what was held back — so they cannot disagree
about what the check carries. Prompt cohort goes to v5.

💄 style(acceptance): make the flow tab readable and stop it moving under the pointer (#19471)

* 💄 style(acceptance): make the flow graph readable at a glance

The flow tab stacks one business flow per group. Four things got in the way

- Branch captions are the only place a transition's condition is written,

- Collapsing or expanding a group re-stacked everything around it and left
  the user looking at whatever slid into its place. The canvas now follows

* 💄 style(acceptance): pin the fullscreen details panel to the right edge

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(acceptance): stop a branch click from throwing the graph across the canvas

Opening the details panel narrows the canvas, and the reveal that followed
called fitView on the selected node, which centres it. Clicking a branch
caption near the right edge therefore moved the whole graph by 220px across
and 463px up: the caption the user had just clicked was no longer anywhere
near the pointer, which reads as the caption disappearing.

Replace both reveals — the one after a panel resize and the one after a group
toggle — with a single minimal pan. It shifts by the least distance that
clears the edge, leaves an axis that already fits untouched, and aligns the
leading edge of anything too large to fit. The same click now moves the
caption 50px across and not at all vertically.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(acceptance): make a branch caption inert instead of a hit target

The edge runs behind its own caption, so a click on the caption landed on the

canvas and shifted the page column — the caption ended up somewhere else and
read as having disappeared. Making the caption itself non-interactive did not

* 💄 style(acceptance): give a branch caption a filled chip instead of an outline

Drop the hairline border for a filled surface. The fill token is translucent,
so it is layered over an opaque one rather than applied directly: the edge
runs underneath the caption, and a translucent background lets the line
strike the text through.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 💄 style(acceptance): lighten the branch caption and clear it of the cards

Two adjustments to the filled caption: drop the fill one step so it reads as a

commits.commit_title: ✨ feat(device-control): list one project directory on demand (#19460)
commits.commit_message:
✨ feat(device-control): list one project directory on demand (#19460)

* ✨ feat(device-control): list one project directory on demand

The project index asks Git for ignored paths with `ls-files --directory`,
which reports a fully ignored folder as a single entry. Its children are
never enumerated, so a caller rendering that entry as an expandable row
has nothing to show.

Mark those entries `collapsed` and add `listProjectDirectory`, which reads
one level of a directory from disk. Callers can then fill a subtree only
when someone opens it, so an ignored folder still costs nothing until then
and `node_modules` is never walked.

The flag is only set when the directory truly has no indexed children — a
nested `.gitignore` that re-includes part of the subtree leaves those rows
complete, and they stay unflagged.

Wired for both transports: an Electron IPC method on the desktop
controller, and a device RPC plus TRPC procedure for remote devices. Also
adds `trashLocalFiles`, which moves paths to the OS trash via
`shell.trashItem` rather than unlinking them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🔒 fix(device-control): resolve symlinks before enforcing project containment

`path.resolve` is lexical, so a symlink that lives inside the project but
points outside it passed the prefix check and then had its target
enumerated. Verified against a real temp fixture: listing a link to an
outside directory returned that directory's files.

Check containment on the real paths of both the root and the target.
Entries are still built from the lexical path, so their ids stay anchored
to the path the caller expanded rather than wherever the link resolved —
a link that stays inside the project keeps working and keeps its row.

Also return per-path outcomes from `trashLocalFiles`. A batch is not
atomic, so bailing out on the first failure left the caller unable to
tell which earlier paths were already in the trash, and therefore unable
to refresh its tree or retry only what was left. This matches the shape
`moveLocalFiles` already returns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.commit_title: 🔒 fix(bot): stop returning bot credentials from the channel list (#19452)
commits.commit_message:
🔒 fix(bot): stop returning bot credentials from the channel list (#19452)

`lh bot list --json` printed every bot's credentials in the clear. In a
workspace that is worse than it sounds: the read path filters on
`workspace_id` alone with no `user_id` term, and the list procedure carries
no write gate, so any member — viewers included — could dump every
colleague's bot token and app secret. That is how a live Feishu app secret
ended up pasted into a chat transcript.

A list is an inventory. It now omits `credentials` entirely, and the detail
read masks each secret instead of returning it.

Masking has to survive the edit form, which reads credentials and submits
them back. The model replaces the credential blob wholesale, so persisting
the mask would destroy the secret and dropping the masked keys would delete
it just the same. `update` therefore resolves every mask back to the stored
value before anything else inspects it, and `create` rejects a mask outright
since a new binding has no secret for it to stand in for.

Which fields are secret comes from the form schema's existing `type:
'password'` marking, so Discord's `publicKey` stays readable while its
`botToken` does not. WeChat fills credentials from its QR handshake and has
no schema to read, so it names its two identifiers through the new
`publicCredentialKeys`. Anything unclassified is treated as secret.

Channel export dropped credentials too, with a line of copy saying so —
exporting masks would have produced a file that looks complete and fails on
import.

commits.commit_title: 🔒 fix(acceptance): close the holes the open discussion opened (#19448)
commits.commit_message:
🔒 fix(acceptance): close the holes the open discussion opened (#19448)

* 🔒 fix(acceptance): close the holes the open discussion opened

Opening an acceptance's discussion to whoever holds its public link widened
three things it should not have.

An agent belongs to its workspace, not to its readers. The author-agent gate
was scoped by the acceptance's workspace, which answers "is this agent
visible there", not "may this caller use it" — and the discussion payload
hands a visitor the ids to pick from. It is now scoped to the workspace only
for callers who actually belong to it; everyone else falls back to their own
agents.

Read-only means read-only. A `viewer` of the acceptance's own workspace was
swept in by "anyone signed in who can read it" and could write on a private
delivery, unlike the same role on topic and document comments. Commenting
now needs the public link or a non-viewer seat.

An open discussion needs a way to close an unwanted remark. Its author is
exactly who will not remove it, so the acceptance's reviewers may now take
one down — the same tombstone the author's own deletion leaves — and a
visitor gets a per-minute ceiling on how much they can land.

Two client reads of `canDelete` as "I wrote this" are replaced by the author
id, since that flag now also turns on for a moderator: whether a thread may
be closed, and whose approval the reviewer bar is showing. The read-only
line no longer flashes while the permission answer is in flight, and the
sign-in return URL moves to a shared helper.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🔒 fix(acceptance): do not call an outside reader a departed teammate

The `former` tag infers "left the workspace" from "is not a member now".
That only holds on a delivery nobody outside could write on. With the link
public, most people in the discussion never had a seat, so the tag is
dropped there rather than guessed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(acceptance): charge the visitor ceiling where the row is written

Codex review of the open-discussion hardening, three findings.

The ceiling was counted before the write and enforced after it, so a burst
of parallel requests each read the same under-limit count and all landed —
which is the shape a flood actually arrives in. It now travels into the
write: the transaction takes an advisory lock on (acceptance, author),
inserts, counts, and rolls itself back when it is the one over the line.
Everybody else still writes in parallel.

The same move fixes a retry being punished for a remark it already made. A
replay of the tenth comment's idempotency key inserts nothing, so it is no
longer counted and answers with the row it wrote the first time, instead of
a refusal for a lost response.

`canResolveThread` reads the signed-in identity, which arrives after the
first paint, but the overlay memo did not depend on it — a thread could keep
the answer computed while nobody was signed in until an unrelated comment
changed. It is a `useCallback` on what it reads, and the memo depends on it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(workbench): let the SSR electron stub answer the gateway device question

Five shared store modules read getElectronStoreState().gatewayDeviceInfo to
decide whether a working directory is local. They enter the workbench SSR graph
through the acceptance check route, where the stub had no such key, so the stub
surface guard failed the build. Give the stub the key with no device, which is
the truthful answer on the server.

commits.commit_title: 🐛 fix(agent-runtime): recover garbled tool names instead of ending the turn (#19362)
commits.commit_message:
🐛 fix(agent-runtime): recover garbled tool names instead of ending the turn (#19362)

* 🐛 fix(agent-runtime): recover garbled tool names instead of ending the turn

When a model garbles the `____` separator in a tool name, `ToolNameResolver`
dropped the call, `GeneralChatAgent` saw no tool calls and no text, and the
operation finished as `done` with an empty assistant message — the conversation
just stops mid-task with no error anywhere.

Observed on tpc_t1n5DfJ0yqtv: glm-5.3-flash emitted
`lobe-local-system~~__runCommand` at step 4 after spelling
`lobe-local-system____runCommand` correctly at steps 0 and 2.

- `ToolNameResolver.resolve` now retries an unresolved call against a squashed
  form of the offered tool names (lowercase, alphanumeric only). Only an
  unambiguous match is accepted, and it runs strictly after the existing
  resolution path, so nothing that resolves today changes.
- When a call still cannot be resolved, `GeneralChatAgent` answers it with a
  rejected tool result (`tool_name_unresolved`) so the model can retry with a
  real name, instead of finishing silently. The feedback is capped at two
  rounds per operation, is skipped once `forceFinish` is set, and falls back to
  throwing so the failure lands on the dashboards as an error.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent-runtime): make the unresolved-tool rejection actually reach the model

Two problems found in review of the previous commit.

The rejected tool rows were written under a parent assistant that carries no
`tools`, so they never came back: state messages are rebuilt from the DB on
every step, and conversation-flow's `collectToolMessages` returns early when
the parent lists no calls. The feedback the model needed was dropped on the way
in. `resolve_blocked_tools` now advertises those calls on the parent before
creating the rows, behind an explicit `unresolvedToolNames` payload flag so the
ordinary allow-list path keeps its single write.

The feedback budget counted matching tool rows in `state.messages`, which is
rehydrated history: rejections from earlier operations spent a new operation's
budget before it started, and two malformed parallel calls consumed both rounds
at once. It is now an operation-scoped counter on `AgentState`, incremented once
per instruction by the executor.

Also names the offending tools in the rejection text. The name the model reads
back from its own turn is regenerated from the persisted identifier/apiName
pair, which for an unparseable name is not what it emitted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* 🐛 fix(agent-runtime): keep the thought signature on unresolvable tool calls

A garbled tool name does not imply a garbled signature. Gemini 3.x attaches
